One adviser was found to have used a personal text messaging application for three client communications in 2023, but the CCO had identified this during a quarterly review, issued a written warning, required the adviser to forward the messages to the archiving system, and updated policies to include additional monitoring of personal device usage.

QUESTION
Did the adviser's remote work compliance framework satisfy regulatory expectations for supervision and recordkeeping given the operational challenges posed by COVID-19 and the hybrid work model?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

The SEC's August 2020 COVID-19 Compliance Risk Alert specifically identified supervision of remote personnel, electronic communications archiving, business continuity planning, and cybersecurity as key compliance risk areas. The firm's proactive implementation of comprehensive supervisory controls directly addresses each of these identified risks. The isolated instance of off-channel communication was detected through the firm's own supervisory review process, promptly remediated, and used as a basis for policy enhancement—demonstrating exactly the type of effective compliance culture that EXAMS expects. The firm's ability to produce complete documentation during examination further demonstrates compliance.

HYPOTHETICAL 585 | COMPLIANT | 05_SEC_Exam_Findings
============================================================

FACTS
An SEC-registered investment adviser with $250 million in AUM provides advisory services to 45 clients over the age of 75, many of whom hold concentrated positions in dividend-paying equities and municipal bonds. In response to SEC EXAMS examination priorities emphasizing protections for senior investors, the firm implemented a Senior Client Protection Program in 2023 that includes: (1) designation of a trusted contact person for each senior client account, (2) enhanced suitability documentation for any portfolio changes involving more than 10% of account value, (3) cognitive assessment protocols where advisers document any observed signs of diminished capacity and escalate to the CCO, (4) a policy permitting temporary holds on disbursements when exploitation is suspected, with mandatory documentation and client notification within two business days, and (5) semi-annual portfolio reviews specifically evaluating liquidity needs, risk tolerance changes, and withdrawal patterns. In January 2025, the firm placed a 48-hour hold on a $95,000 wire transfer from the account of an 82-year-old client after the assigned adviser noted the request was inconsistent with the client's typical activity and the client appeared confused about the destination of the funds. The CCO contacted the designated trusted contact person—the client's adult daughter—who confirmed she was unaware of the transfer. The hold was documented, the client was notified in writing within one business day, and the matter was referred to Adult Protective Services. The wire was ultimately not processed after the client, upon further reflection with family present, confirmed she had been contacted by an unknown party requesting the funds.

QUESTION
Did the adviser's senior investor protection protocols and temporary disbursement hold comply with regulatory expectations and fiduciary obligations, or did the hold constitute an improper restriction on the client's account access?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

SEC EXAMS has consistently identified protection of senior investors as a priority examination focus, and the framework established by FINRA Rule 2165 provides a regulatory blueprint for temporary holds when financial exploitation is reasonably suspected. The adviser's actions were proportionate—a 48-hour hold with prompt documentation, client notification within one business day, contact with the designated trusted contact, and referral to Adult Protective Services. The firm's broader Senior Client Protection Program demonstrates systematic compliance with examination priorities rather than ad hoc decision-making. The temporary restriction on account access was a reasonable exercise of fiduciary duty to protect a vulnerable client from suspected exploitation, not an improper limitation.

Does Samantha's annuity recommendation to an IRA holder comply with PTE 2020-02 despite the conflicted compensation arrangement?

PTE 2020-02 permits investment advice fiduciaries to receive conflicted compensation provided they satisfy all exemption conditions: rendering advice in the client's best interest reflecting care, skill, and prudence; charging no more than reasonable compensation; making required disclosures of conflicts and compensation; and maintaining written policies and procedures subject to retrospective review. The family office employs a CFA-credentialed chief investment officer, has its own compliance infrastructure, and meets the definition of a 'family office' under Rule 202(a)(11)(G)-1 of the Advisers Act. When Meridian's registered representatives recommend a portfolio of structured notes and alternative credit funds to the Harrington Family Office, the firm does not apply its standard Regulation Best Interest documentation and disclosure procedures — including Form CRS delivery — that it uses for retail customers. Meridian relies on the SIFMA no-action letter dated December 23, 2020, treating the Harrington Family Office as an 'Institutional Family Office' rather than a 'retail customer' for Reg BI purposes, after confirming the family office meets all conditions specified in the no-action letter, including that it has at least $50 million in assets under management and is staffed by individuals with sufficient financial sophistication to evaluate the recommendations independently.

QUESTION
Is Meridian Wealth Partners compliant in not applying Regulation Best Interest retail customer obligations when making recommendations to the Harrington Family Office?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

The December 23, 2020 SIFMA no-action letter provides assurance that Staff would not recommend enforcement action against broker-dealers that do not treat qualifying 'Institutional Family Offices' as 'retail customers' for purposes of Reg BI and Form CRS. The Harrington Family Office meets the conditions described in the letter: it qualifies as a family office under Advisers Act Rule 202(a)(11)(G)-1, manages substantial assets, and employs financially sophisticated personnel. Because Meridian verified all qualifying conditions before relying on the no-action position, its decision not to apply Reg BI retail customer procedures is consistent with the Staff's stated position.

HYPOTHETICAL 602 | NON-COMPLIANT | 01_SEC_Guidance_NoAction_Interpretive
============================================================

FACTS
Greenfield Advisory Group, a registered investment adviser managing $120 million in assets, recently received several positive reviews from existing clients on an independent third-party review site, WealthAdvisorReviews.com. Greenfield's marketing director copies and pastes three of the most glowing five-star client reviews — including specific claims such as 'Greenfield doubled my portfolio in two years' and 'Best adviser I've ever worked with, guaranteed returns' — directly onto the firm's own website and includes them in a PDF brochure emailed to 2,000 prospective clients. The firm does not add any disclaimers, does not disclose whether the reviewers were compensated, and does not present any reviews that are less favorable. The marketing materials were distributed in September 2021, prior to the November 4, 2022 effective date of the new SEC Marketing Rule (Rule 206(4)-1), meaning the prior testimonial prohibition under the old Advisers Act advertising rule was still in effect.

QUESTION
Was Greenfield Advisory Group compliant when it republished selected client testimonials from a third-party review site onto its own website and marketing brochure in September 2021?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is a violation of the testimonial prohibition under the former Advisers Act advertising rule.

Under the pre-November 2022 advertising rule, investment advisers were prohibited from using testimonials in their advertisements. IM Guidance Update 2014-04 recognized that while third-party commentary may appear organically on independent social media sites, an adviser's affirmative act of republishing selected favorable testimonials onto its own website and distributing them in marketing materials constitutes the use of testimonials in an advertisement. Greenfield's cherry-picking of only the most favorable reviews, including one referencing 'guaranteed returns,' and distributing them without any context or balance, directly violated the then-operative testimonial prohibition.

HYPOTHETICAL 603 | NON-COMPLIANT | 02_SEC_Enforcement_Actions
============================================================

FACTS
Heartland Advisory Group, LLC, a registered investment adviser managing approximately $420 million in client assets, maintained a dual-hatted arrangement where its principal, David Renner, also served as a licensed insurance agent. From 2018 through 2021, Renner directed over 140 advisory clients—predominantly retirees with moderate risk tolerances and account sizes averaging $285,000—into proprietary variable annuity products underwritten by an affiliated insurance company. These variable annuities carried surrender periods of 7 years and internal expenses of 2.85% annually, whereas substantially similar non-affiliated variable annuity products were available with internal expenses of 1.40% and 4-year surrender periods. Heartland's Form ADV Part 2A disclosed that 'affiliates may receive compensation in connection with certain insurance products,' but did not specify the magnitude of the conflict, the revenue-sharing arrangement with the affiliated insurer, or that lower-cost alternatives existed. Heartland received approximately $1.9 million in additional revenue from the affiliated insurer over the three-year period.

QUESTION
Did Heartland Advisory Group violate its fiduciary obligations under the Investment Advisers Act by placing clients in higher-cost affiliated variable annuities without adequate disclosure of the conflict of interest?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is not compliant. This constitutes a violation of Sections 206(1) and 206(2) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 for breach of fiduciary duty through inadequate conflict-of-interest disclosure and failure to act in clients' best interests.

Under Sections 206(1) and 206(2) of the Advisers Act, an investment adviser owes a fiduciary duty to its clients that includes both a duty of care and a duty of loyalty, which requires full and fair disclosure of all material conflicts of interest. As seen in SEC enforcement actions against firms like VisionPoint Advisory Group (IA-4778), Summit Financial Group (IA-5168), and First Citizens Asset Management (IA-5123), the Commission has consistently held that boilerplate or generic disclosures about affiliate compensation are insufficient when the adviser is systematically steering clients into higher-cost affiliated products. The $1.9 million in undisclosed revenue from the affiliated insurer constitutes a material conflict that a reasonable client would want to know about when evaluating the adviser's recommendation, and the failure to disclose available lower-cost alternatives compounded the breach of the duty of care.

HYPOTHETICAL 604 | COMPLIANT | 02_SEC_Enforcement_Actions
============================================================

FACTS
Lakeview Wealth Partners, LLC, a registered investment adviser with $310 million in assets under management, allocates a portion of certain client portfolios to a private real estate fund managed by an affiliated entity in which Lakeview's founder holds a 30% ownership interest. The allocation is limited to clients with liquid net worth exceeding $2 million and investable assets above $1 million, and no client has more than 8% of their total portfolio allocated to the affiliated fund. Lakeview's Form ADV Part 2A contains a dedicated section titled 'Affiliated Fund Conflict of Interest' that specifically identifies the founder's ownership stake, quantifies the additional management fee layer (0.75% annually) charged by the affiliated fund, explains that the allocation creates an incentive for Lakeview to recommend the fund over non-affiliated alternatives, and lists three comparable non-affiliated real estate funds with their respective fee structures. Each affected client received a standalone written conflict disclosure at the time of the initial allocation, signed an acknowledgment, and was offered the option to opt out and instead invest in one of the identified non-affiliated alternatives. Lakeview's compliance department conducts quarterly reviews of affiliated fund allocations and documents the investment rationale for each client based on individual investment policy statements.

QUESTION
Does Lakeview Wealth Partners' practice of allocating client assets to an affiliated private real estate fund comply with its fiduciary obligations under the Investment Advisers Act given the inherent conflict of interest?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

While allocating client assets to an affiliated fund creates an inherent conflict of interest, the Advisers Act does not categorically prohibit such arrangements—it requires that the adviser provide full and fair disclosure sufficient for the client to provide informed consent. Lakeview's approach addresses the specific deficiencies the SEC has targeted in enforcement actions against firms like VisionPoint (IA-4778) and Michigan Advisors (IA-5395): the disclosure is specific rather than generic, it quantifies the additional cost layer, it identifies the economic incentive, it names comparable alternatives, and each client affirmatively consented after receiving a standalone written notice. The 8% portfolio concentration limit, suitability screening for high-net-worth clients, and quarterly compliance reviews further demonstrate that the duty of care was met through reasonable diligence and ongoing monitoring of the recommendation's appropriateness.

HYPOTHETICAL 605 | NON-COMPLIANT | 07_Practitioner_Commentary
============================================================

FACTS
A mid-size broker-dealer with 180 registered representatives implements Regulation Best Interest compliance policies on June 30, 2020, the effective date. However, the firm's compliance program consists solely of distributing a written Reg BI policy manual to representatives via email, with no live training sessions, no assessments, and no mechanism to verify that representatives read or understood the materials. A 72-year-old retired teacher is subsequently recommended a high-commission variable annuity with a 7-year surrender period by a representative who, when questioned in a subsequent examination, cannot articulate the basic components of the Care Obligation or explain why the annuity was in the client's best interest. The SEC Division of Examinations identifies this deficiency during a routine exam aligned with its stated priorities of reviewing Reg BI compliance programs.

QUESTION
Did the broker-dealer satisfy its supervisory and compliance obligations under Reg BI by distributing a written policy manual without conducting training or verifying representative understanding?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is a violation of the firm's Reg BI Compliance Obligation and FINRA supervisory requirements.

The Reg BI Compliance Obligation requires broker-dealers to establish, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to achieve compliance with Reg BI. Merely distributing a manual without training, testing, or follow-up monitoring is not reasonably designed to achieve compliance. FINRA Rule 3110 similarly requires firms to supervise their associated persons' activities, which includes ensuring they are adequately trained on applicable regulatory obligations. The SEC's Division of Examinations has specifically identified Reg BI compliance program design and implementation as examination priorities.

Fourteen months after their initial registration, none of the five representatives have completed the Regulatory Element of CE. FINRA Regulatory Notice 17-30 approved amendments to CE requirements alongside the restructured SIE and top-off examination framework, reinforcing the importance of ongoing education for registered representatives. FINRA Rule 1240 requires registered persons to complete the Regulatory Element of CE within prescribed timeframes, and failure to do so results in inactive status, meaning the representatives should not have been permitted to continue performing registered activities. The firm's decision to allow these representatives to continue recommending complex structured products without completed CE also violates FINRA Rule 3110's requirement for a supervisory system reasonably designed to ensure compliance with applicable securities laws and regulations.

HYPOTHETICAL 608 | NON-COMPLIANT | 07_Practitioner_Commentary

FACTS

The SEC Division of Examinations has specifically identified Form PF reporting accuracy and timeliness as a 2026 examination priority, indicating heightened scrutiny of exactly this type of deficiency. HYPOTHETICAL 609 | COMPLIANT | 07_Practitioner_Commentary
============================================================

FACTS
A broker-dealer with 500 registered representatives implements a comprehensive Reg BI compliance program that includes: (1) annual in-person training modules covering the Care, Disclosure, Conflict of Interest, and Compliance Obligations; (2) quarterly assessments where representatives must demonstrate, using recent client case studies, how they evaluated reasonably available alternatives before making recommendations; (3) an automated surveillance system that flags recommendations of high-cost products to clients over age 65 or with conservative risk profiles for supervisory review; and (4) an enhanced conflict-of-interest inventory updated semi-annually that maps revenue-sharing arrangements, proprietary product incentives, and compensation differentials. A 68-year-old retiree with a moderate risk tolerance is recommended a B-share mutual fund. The automated system flags the recommendation, a supervisor reviews it, and after confirming that the B-share's lower upfront cost and the client's stated 8-year holding period make it cost-effective compared to A-share and C-share alternatives, the supervisor approves the transaction with documented rationale.

QUESTION
Does the broker-dealer's compliance program and the specific supervisory review of the B-share recommendation satisfy Reg BI's Compliance and Care Obligations?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

The firm's multi-layered compliance program—featuring training, assessments, automated surveillance, and a detailed conflict-of-interest inventory—is reasonably designed to achieve compliance with all four Reg BI component obligations. The specific supervisory review of the B-share recommendation demonstrates the Care Obligation in action: the supervisor evaluated reasonably available alternatives (A-shares, C-shares) and documented why the B-share was in the client's best interest given her 8-year holding period and preference for lower upfront costs. This reflects the kind of robust compliance infrastructure that industry guidance from SIFMA and examination priorities from the SEC Division of Examinations envision.

HYPOTHETICAL 610 | NON-COMPLIANT | 03_FINRA_AWC
============================================================

FACTS
Pinnacle Financial Services, Inc., a FINRA member firm since 2001 headquartered in Monaca, Pennsylvania, offers various investment products including deferred variable annuities through its approximately 260 registered representatives across more than 180 branch offices. From January 2018 through December 2022, the firm's supervisory system, including its written supervisory procedures (WSPs), failed to reasonably supervise variable annuity exchange transactions. The firm's WSPs did not require supervisors to document a meaningful comparison of the costs, features, and surrender periods of the existing annuity versus the recommended replacement annuity before approving exchanges. During this period, registered representative Kevin Dorsey recommended 47 variable annuity exchanges for 31 customers — predominantly retirees aged 65-78 with moderate risk tolerances and account values ranging from $85,000 to $340,000 — into new annuity contracts carrying fresh 7-year surrender periods and total annual fees averaging 45 basis points higher than the surrendered contracts. The firm's principal reviewers approved all 47 exchanges using a checklist that did not require any quantitative cost comparison, and the firm had no automated surveillance system to flag exchanges where the new product's costs exceeded the existing product's costs.

QUESTION
Did Pinnacle Financial Services maintain a supervisory system reasonably designed to supervise its registered representatives' variable annuity exchange recommendations?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is a supervision violation under FINRA Rules 3110 and 2010.

FINRA Rule 3110 requires member firms to establish and maintain a system to supervise the activities of each associated person that is reasonably designed to achieve compliance with applicable securities laws and regulations. The firm's WSPs failed to require principals to conduct or document any meaningful quantitative comparison of existing versus replacement variable annuity costs, features, and surrender schedules before approving exchanges. This mirrors the pattern identified in the Fortune Financial Services AWC, where a firm's supervisory system was found deficient for failing to reasonably supervise variable annuity transactions over a multi-year period. The absence of automated surveillance tools or documented cost-comparison requirements rendered the firm's supervisory framework inadequate.

HYPOTHETICAL 611 | COMPLIANT | 03_FINRA_AWC
============================================================

FACTS
Maria Vasquez, a registered representative at Clearview Securities LLC since 2015, recommends that her client Thomas Hargrove, age 62, exchange his existing deferred variable annuity (current value $210,000, 2 years remaining on a 7-year surrender period, total annual expenses of 2.15%) into a new variable annuity with a guaranteed lifetime withdrawal benefit rider (total annual expenses of 2.55%, new 6-year surrender period). Hargrove, a recently retired municipal worker with a $48,000 annual pension, $390,000 in total investable assets, and a moderate risk tolerance, has expressed significant concern about outliving his retirement savings and specifically requested income guarantees. Vasquez documents a detailed comparison showing the existing annuity lacks any living benefit rider, that the 40-basis-point cost increase funds the guaranteed withdrawal benefit valued at 5% annual withdrawals for life beginning at age 65, and that Hargrove's surrender charge on the existing contract ($4,200) is substantially offset by the new carrier's enhanced death benefit. The firm's principal reviewer independently verifies the suitability analysis, confirms the client's stated objective of lifetime income, reviews the cost comparison, and documents approval with a written rationale referencing Hargrove's specific retirement income gap.

QUESTION
Was Vasquez's recommendation to exchange the existing variable annuity for a new contract with higher fees and a new surrender period suitable and compliant with applicable standards?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

Although the exchange involves higher annual costs and a new surrender period — factors that typically warrant heightened scrutiny — the recommendation is grounded in the client's specific, documented need for guaranteed lifetime income that the existing contract cannot provide. Under both FINRA Rule 2111's reasonable-basis and customer-specific suitability components, and Reg BI's Care Obligation, a recommendation may involve higher costs if the overall benefits to the particular customer justify the expense. The representative conducted and documented a thorough cost-benefit comparison, the client's income gap and stated objectives supported the guaranteed withdrawal feature, and the firm's principal independently reviewed and approved the transaction with written rationale — satisfying both the suitability and supervisory requirements.

HYPOTHETICAL 612 | NON-COMPLIANT | 04_RegBI_Compliance_Guidance
============================================================

FACTS
Marcus Henley, a registered representative at a small broker-dealer with 30 registered representatives, recommended that seven retail customers invest a combined $385,000 in pre-IPO private placement interests in three early-stage technology companies between January 2021 and June 2021. Henley sourced the offerings and brought them to his firm for approval. In connection with each offering, Henley received a selling compensation of 15%, which exceeded the 10% maximum disclosed in the offering memoranda provided to customers. Henley did not disclose the additional 5% compensation to any of the seven customers, nor did he document any analysis of the risks, rewards, and costs of the private placements relative to other reasonably available alternatives. Several of the customers were retirees with moderate risk tolerances and annual incomes under $75,000.

QUESTION
Did the registered representative comply with Regulation Best Interest's Disclosure and Care Obligations when recommending these private placement interests?

ANSWER
No, this conduct violates the Reg BI Disclosure Obligation and Care Obligation.

Under the Reg BI Disclosure Obligation, the representative was required to provide full and fair disclosure of all material facts relating to the scope and terms of the relationship, including all compensation received in connection with the recommendation. Receiving compensation 50% above the disclosed maximum in the offering documents and failing to disclose this to customers is a material omission. Additionally, the Care Obligation required Henley to exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill to have a reasonable basis to believe each recommendation was in the customer's best interest, including understanding the risks, rewards, and costs. Recommending illiquid, high-risk pre-IPO private placements to retirees with moderate risk tolerances and modest incomes without documented analysis of these factors or consideration of alternatives fails the Care Obligation. This fact pattern closely mirrors the FINRA complaint against Gustave Schmidt (No. 2022074096805).

HYPOTHETICAL 613 | COMPLIANT | 04_RegBI_Compliance_Guidance
============================================================

FACTS
Jennifer Dao, a financial professional at a mid-sized broker-dealer, recommended that her client, Robert Engel (age 58, annual income $210,000, liquid net worth $1.4 million, moderate-to-aggressive risk tolerance, stated goal of growth before retirement in seven years), allocate $200,000 from a maturing CD into a diversified portfolio comprising a Class A mutual fund (equity growth fund with a 4.25% front-end load and a 0.72% expense ratio) and a no-load intermediate-term bond fund (0.45% expense ratio). Dao documented her consideration of three reasonably available alternatives: a lower-cost ETF portfolio, an advisory wrap account at a 1.25% annual fee, and a variable annuity with a 1.35% M&E charge and 7-year surrender period. In her written rationale, Dao explained that the Class A share breakpoint at $200,000 reduced the effective load, the client's preference for a commission-based transactional relationship and infrequent trading made the Class A share more cost-effective over the client's seven-year horizon than the wrap account, and that the variable annuity's surrender charges and higher ongoing costs were not justified given the client's timeline. Dao's firm had policies requiring documented cost comparisons for share-class recommendations and had conducted annual compliance reviews confirming enforcement of these policies.

QUESTION
Did the financial professional satisfy the Reg BI Care Obligation when recommending the Class A mutual fund over lower-cost alternatives?

Yes, this conduct is compliant.

The Care Obligation requires that a financial professional exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill to understand the potential risks, rewards, and costs of a recommendation and have a reasonable basis to believe it is in the retail customer's best interest in light of the customer's investment profile. The SEC's January 2023 Risk Alert specifically flagged deficiencies where firms failed to consider reasonably available alternatives or to document cost comparisons, particularly for share-class recommendations. Here, Dao documented her evaluation of three alternatives with specific cost and suitability analysis, matched the recommendation to the client's profile (growth objective, seven-year horizon, preference for transactional relationship), and utilized available breakpoints to reduce costs. The firm's written supervisory procedures requiring cost comparisons and its annual compliance reviews further demonstrate satisfaction of the Compliance Obligation under Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(iv).

HYPOTHETICAL 615 | COMPLIANT | 05_SEC_Exam_Findings
============================================================

FACTS

During the Division of Examinations' review — reflecting 2022 and 2025 exam priorities targeting wrap fee program suitability — examiners note that the client's trading frequency could suggest the wrap fee is cost-effective compared to a per-transaction commission model. The adviser maintains a quarterly suitability review process that documents the client's trading activity, compares annualized wrap costs ($18,000) against estimated per-trade commission costs (estimated at $24.80 per trade × 62 trades = $1,537.60 in commissions alone, plus a standalone advisory fee of approximately 1.00%, totaling roughly $13,538), showing the wrap program costs approximately $4,462 more per year. However, the adviser's documentation explains that the wrap fee also bundles research access, unlimited financial planning consultations, and tax-loss harvesting services the client actively uses, and the client signed an updated disclosure acknowledging the cost differential and affirming the value of bundled services after an annual best-interest review meeting.

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

SEC exam priorities have consistently flagged wrap fee programs where clients trade infrequently and would pay less under a transaction-based model, making the wrap fee effectively a reverse churning concern. Here, however, the adviser conducted and documented a thorough cost-benefit analysis, disclosed the cost differential transparently to the client, and demonstrated that bundled services — including tax-loss harvesting, financial planning, and research access actively utilized by the client — provide value beyond mere trade execution. The client's informed, documented consent after a clear comparison satisfies the adviser's fiduciary obligation to act in the client's best interest and to make full and fair disclosure of material conflicts.

HYPOTHETICAL 616 | NON-COMPLIANT | 06_DOL_Fiduciary
============================================================

FACTS
Maria Gonzalez, age 58, has a 401(k) plan with her employer containing $340,000 in low-cost index funds with an all-in expense ratio of 0.04%. Her financial advisor, Greg Paulson, recommends she roll the entire balance into an IRA at his broker-dealer, where he places her in a portfolio of actively managed mutual funds with an average expense ratio of 1.35% and a 5.25% front-end sales load. Greg earns a $12,750 commission on the rollover transaction. Greg does not document any comparison of the fees, investment options, or services available in Maria's existing 401(k) plan versus the proposed IRA, nor does he consider that Maria could leave her assets in the 401(k) plan at no additional cost. Greg's firm has no written rollover analysis policy.

QUESTION
Did the advisor satisfy DOL fiduciary obligations and PTE 2020-02 requirements when recommending this 401(k)-to-IRA rollover?

PTE 2020-02 requires that investment advice fiduciaries recommending rollovers must act in the retirement investor's best interest and provide recommendations that reflect the care, skill, and prudence of a knowledgeable professional. The exemption specifically requires documentation of the bases for a rollover recommendation, including a comparison of fees, services, and investment options between the existing plan and the proposed IRA. Greg failed to perform or document any such comparative analysis, and the dramatically higher costs in the IRA (1.35% expense ratio plus a 5.25% load versus 0.04%) strongly suggest the recommendation was driven by his $12,750 commission rather than Maria's best interest.

HYPOTHETICAL 617 | NON-COMPLIANT | 06_DOL_Fiduciary
============================================================

FACTS
James Liu, age 64 and recently retired, has $520,000 in a traditional IRA. His advisor, Stephanie Wells, who operates under a dual-registered broker-dealer and RIA, recommends James invest $310,000 in a non-traded REIT with a 7-year lock-up period and 12% upfront commission, and $150,000 in a fixed indexed annuity paying her a 7% commission. Stephanie provides James a written disclosure acknowledging her firm's material conflicts of interest and the compensation she will receive. Stephanie's individual recommendation documentation states the products are 'suitable for a retiree seeking income' but contains no analysis of lower-cost alternatives or liquidity needs.

QUESTION
Does the advisor's conduct satisfy the conditions of PTE 2020-02 for relying on the exemption from prohibited transaction rules under ERISA and IRC §4975?

ANSWER
No, this conduct violates PTE 2020-02's conditions requiring retrospective compliance reviews, updated written policies, and a best interest recommendation standard that goes beyond mere suitability.

PTE 2020-02 conditions relief from prohibited transaction provisions on several cumulative requirements: the advice must satisfy Impartial Conduct Standards (best interest, reasonable compensation, no materially misleading statements), the financial institution must maintain written policies and procedures that are current, and the institution must conduct a retrospective compliance review at least annually. Stephanie's firm has failed to conduct the required retrospective review for two years and has not updated its written policies since before PTE 2020-02 took effect. Additionally, stating the products are merely 'suitable' without analyzing lower-cost alternatives or James's liquidity needs fails the best interest standard, which requires more than traditional suitability analysis.

HYPOTHETICAL 618 | COMPLIANT | 06_DOL_Fiduciary
============================================================

FACTS
Rachel Kim is the HR Director and named ERISA fiduciary for a small employer's 401(k) plan with $8.2 million in assets and 74 participants. The plan is terminating because the company is shutting down. After extensive efforts to locate all participants, the plan has $47,000 in account balances belonging to 6 participants who cannot be found despite certified mail, email outreach, a commercial locator service, and searching the Social Security Administration's letter-forwarding program. Rachel, after consulting with the plan's ERISA counsel, elects to transfer the missing participants' balances to the PBGC's Missing Participants Program for terminating defined contribution plans. She documents each search step taken and the decision rationale in the plan's termination file. No distributions are made to an IRA rollover provider with whom the firm has a revenue-sharing arrangement.

QUESTION
Did the plan fiduciary act consistently with ERISA fiduciary duties when transferring missing participants' balances to the PBGC Missing Participants Program upon plan termination?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

DOL FAB 2021-01 establishes a temporary enforcement policy under which the Department will not pursue fiduciary breach claims against plan fiduciaries of terminating defined contribution plans who transfer missing participants' balances to the PBGC's expanded Missing Participants Program, provided the fiduciary has conducted reasonable, documented search efforts. Rachel conducted multiple search methods, documented each step, consulted with ERISA counsel, and chose the PBGC program rather than a self-interested IRA rollover arrangement. This conduct falls squarely within the safe harbor and the DOL's temporary enforcement policy, satisfying ERISA §404(a)(1)'s prudence standard.

HYPOTHETICAL 619 | NON-COMPLIANT | 06_DOL_Fiduciary
============================================================

FACTS
David Carpenter, a registered representative at a large independent broker-dealer, provides a one-time recommendation to Patricia Owens, age 71, that she transfer $275,000 from her existing IRA at Vanguard — invested in a diversified portfolio of index funds with a 0.07% weighted average expense ratio — into a variable annuity with a guaranteed minimum income benefit rider. The variable annuity has total annual fees of 3.15% (including mortality and expense charges, sub-account fees, and the rider fee) and a 7-year declining surrender charge schedule starting at 8%. David's firm acknowledges he is a fiduciary under the DOL's expanded definition because the recommendation is made in a professional capacity, for a fee, and Patricia relies on it as a basis for her investment decision. David provides Patricia a written disclosure of his compensation and conflicts, and his firm has current written policies and has conducted its most recent retrospective review. However, David's documentation states only that Patricia 'expressed interest in guaranteed income,' without any analysis of whether the annuity's cost is justified relative to lower-cost alternatives such as a systematic withdrawal strategy from her existing index fund portfolio, or whether the surrender charges are appropriate given Patricia's age and potential need for liquidity.

QUESTION
Does the advisor's rollover recommendation from a low-cost IRA to a high-cost variable annuity satisfy the Impartial Conduct Standards under PTE 2020-02, even though the firm has otherwise satisfied the exemption's procedural conditions?

ANSWER
No, this conduct violates PTE 2020-02's Impartial Conduct Standards, specifically the best interest obligation requiring consideration of reasonably available alternatives and cost.

While David's firm has satisfied the procedural conditions of PTE 2020-02 (written policies, retrospective review, disclosure), the exemption also requires that each individual recommendation satisfy the Impartial Conduct Standards. The best interest standard demands that the fiduciary exercise the care, skill, and prudence of a knowledgeable professional and consider the costs and reasonably available alternatives. Documenting only that the client 'expressed interest in guaranteed income' without analyzing whether the 3.15% all-in annuity cost is justified relative to lower-cost income strategies, or whether the 8% surrender charge is appropriate for a 71-year-old with potential liquidity needs, fails this standard. Satisfying the procedural conditions of PTE 2020-02 does not excuse a substantively deficient recommendation.

HYPOTHETICAL 620 | COMPLIANT | 06_DOL_Fiduciary
============================================================

FACTS
Angela Torres, a fee-based financial advisor at a dually registered firm, recommends that her client Robert Dunn, age 55, roll $190,000 from his former employer's 401(k) plan into an IRA managed by Angela on a fee-based advisory platform charging 0.90% annually. Robert's 401(k) plan offers only 12 investment options, has limited online tools, and charges a 0.85% total plan expense (including administrative fees and fund expenses). Angela prepares a detailed written rollover analysis comparing the 401(k) plan's investment menu, fees, and services with the IRA's broader investment options (including ETFs, individual bonds, and model portfolios), personalized financial planning services, and tax-loss harvesting capabilities. The analysis documents that the slight fee increase of 0.05% is offset by substantially broader investment choices, personalized advice, and integrated estate and tax planning. Angela's firm has current PTE 2020-02 compliant written policies, provides full disclosure of her advisory fee and material conflicts, and conducted its annual retrospective review three months prior.

QUESTION
Is the advisor's rollover recommendation from a 401(k) to a slightly higher-cost fee-based IRA compliant with PTE 2020-02 given the marginal cost increase?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

PTE 2020-02's best interest standard does not require that the lowest-cost option always be recommended; rather, it requires that the fiduciary prudently analyze and document why the recommendation serves the retirement investor's best interest considering all relevant factors including investment options, fees, services, and the investor's specific needs. Angela prepared a thorough comparative analysis documenting that the marginal 0.05% fee increase is justified by materially broader investment options, personalized financial planning, and tax-optimization services unavailable in the 401(k). Her firm has also satisfied all procedural conditions — current written policies, conflict disclosures, and a recent retrospective review. This represents a well-documented, substantively justified rollover recommendation.

HYPOTHETICAL 625 | NON-COMPLIANT | 07_Practitioner_Commentary

FACTS

The firm maintained a revenue-sharing arrangement with three product sponsors—Apex Growth Fund, Sentinel Income Trust, and Vanguard Strategic Allocation—that paid Pinnacle between 25 and 40 basis points annually on assets placed by its representatives. These arrangements were disclosed in a general conflicts section of the firm's Form CRS, which stated: 'We receive compensation from certain product sponsors, which creates a conflict of interest.' The firm's supervisory system flagged no alerts because it was not programmed to monitor for concentration in high-revenue-share products.

QUESTION
Did Pinnacle Financial Partners satisfy the Reg BI Conflict of Interest Obligation and Disclosure Obligation with respect to its revenue-sharing arrangements and the resulting recommendations?

The FINRA Reg BI Checklist makes clear that the best interest standard is satisfied only if the firm complies with all four component obligations, including Conflict of Interest and Disclosure. The Conflict of Interest Obligation requires firms to establish written policies and procedures reasonably designed to identify, disclose, and mitigate or eliminate conflicts, including those arising from revenue-sharing arrangements that incentivize representatives to recommend particular products. Pinnacle's deliberate omission of Conflict of Interest training, its failure to program supervisory systems to detect concentration in high-revenue-share products, and its generic Form CRS disclosure that omitted the specific products, compensation range, and mitigation measures all fall short of both the Conflict of Interest and Disclosure Obligations. The pattern of 87 recommendations concentrated in the highest-paying product further evidences the unmitigated conflict.

Without obtaining prior written consent or making any disclosure, the representative arranges cross-trades between two client accounts—selling 5,000 shares of a mid-cap equity from Client A's account to Client B's account at the prior day's closing price—to rebalance both portfolios. The representative believes the trade benefits both clients and charges no additional commission, but no written authorization for principal or agency cross-transactions exists in either client's advisory agreement.

QUESTION
Does this cross-trade arrangement comply with the NASAA Model Rule on unethical business practices of investment advisers?

ANSWER
No, this conduct constitutes an unethical business practice under NASAA Model Rule 102(a)(4)-1.

NASAA Model Rule 102(a)(4)-1 establishes that investment advisers and their representatives are fiduciaries who must act primarily for the benefit of their clients. Effecting cross-trades between discretionary client accounts without prior written disclosure and client consent violates the fiduciary duty of loyalty and the prohibition on conflicts of interest. Even if the adviser subjectively believes the trade benefits both parties, the absence of informed consent and written authorization makes this an unethical business practice under the rule.

James earns a modest 25-basis-point trail commission on the proprietary funds. Before making the recommendation, James documents a detailed analysis showing that Robert's money market position yields effectively 0% real return after inflation, that Robert needs growth to sustain a 30-year retirement, and that the proprietary funds have consistently ranked in the top quartile of their Morningstar categories over 10 years. The firm maintains written policies and procedures under PTE 2020-02, disclosed all material conflicts including the affiliation and trail compensation in writing to Robert before the transaction, conducted a retrospective compliance review of James's rollover and reallocation recommendations in the prior quarter, and James acknowledged the firm's fiduciary status in the written disclosure.

QUESTION
Does the advisor's recommendation of proprietary mutual funds for the IRA, which generate trail compensation for the advisor, comply with PTE 2020-02 despite the inherent conflict of interest?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

PTE 2020-02 does not prohibit conflicted compensation or recommendations of proprietary products; rather, it requires that such recommendations satisfy the Impartial Conduct Standards, meaning the advice must be in the retirement investor's best interest, compensation must be reasonable, and the fiduciary must not make materially misleading statements. Here, the advisor documented a thorough analysis demonstrating the suitability and best-interest basis for the recommendation (addressing Robert's need for real returns over a long retirement horizon), the proprietary funds were competitively priced relative to comparable active alternatives and had strong track records, and the firm made full written disclosure of the affiliated relationship and compensation. The firm's written policies, retrospective review program, and acknowledgment of fiduciary status satisfy PTE 2020-02's additional procedural conditions, thereby preserving the exemption despite the surface appearance of conflict.

HYPOTHETICAL 658 | NON-COMPLIANT | 07_Practitioner_Commentary
============================================================

FACTS
A mid-sized broker-dealer serves a mix of retail and institutional clients. In late 2020, the firm's compliance department received guidance from SIFMA regarding the treatment of family offices under Reg BI, specifically that qualifying 'Institutional Family Offices' need not be treated as 'retail customers.' Based on this guidance, the firm's Chief Compliance Officer issued a blanket internal policy directing all registered representatives to classify every family office client — regardless of size, sophistication, or qualifying status — as institutional, thereby exempting all family office recommendations from Reg BI's Care, Disclosure, and Conflict of Interest obligations. The firm did not perform any individualized analysis to determine whether each family office met the specific conditions outlined in the SIFMA no-action request, such as whether the family office qualified under the Investment Advisers Act Section 202(a)(11)(G) exemption and managed at least $5 million in assets. One such family office, the Hernandez Family Office, manages approximately $1.2 million for a single household and has no dedicated investment professionals on staff. A representative recommended a complex structured note with a 4.5% upfront commission to this family office without providing a Form CRS or conducting a best interest analysis.

QUESTION
Did the broker-dealer's blanket policy exempting all family office clients from Reg BI retail customer protections comply with applicable regulatory standards?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is a violation of Reg BI's Care and Disclosure Obligations and reflects a failure of reasonable compliance program design.

The SIFMA no-action letter regarding Institutional Family Offices was predicated on specific qualifying conditions — including that the family office meet the criteria under the Advisers Act exemption and possess sufficient sophistication and assets. The firm's blanket policy failed to conduct the individualized analysis required by the no-action letter's conditions. The Hernandez Family Office, with only $1.2 million in assets and no dedicated investment staff, would not qualify as an Institutional Family Office under these conditions and therefore must be treated as a retail customer entitled to full Reg BI protections, including Form CRS delivery and a best interest analysis before any recommendation.

============================================================

FACTS
Ahead of the June 2020 Reg BI compliance date, a regional broker-dealer with 85 registered representatives implemented a comprehensive compliance program. The firm's 12-hour training program, updated Form CRS conforming to the SEC's prescribed format and conversation starters as described in industry FAQs, timely delivery protocol, monthly supervisory reviews of recommendations, and explicit conflict-of-interest policies collectively demonstrate a reasonably designed compliance program. The firm's approach aligns with SIFMA and industry guidance emphasizing that firms should train representatives on all four Reg BI obligations and update supervisory procedures to monitor ongoing compliance.

HYPOTHETICAL 660 | NON-COMPLIANT | 08_State_Fiduciary_Rules
============================================================

FACTS
A New York-based insurance producer recommends that a 72-year-old retired widow replace her existing fixed annuity (earning 3.2% with no surrender charges remaining) with a new indexed annuity carrying a 10-year surrender period and a 7% surrender charge in year one. The client has $185,000 in liquid savings, a modest Social Security income of $1,850/month, and has expressed a primary goal of preserving principal for healthcare expenses. The producer earns an 8% first-year commission on the new indexed annuity versus 0% trailing commission on the existing product. The producer documents the client's risk tolerance as 'moderate growth' but does not document any analysis of why the replacement is in the client's best interest compared to retaining the existing annuity, nor does he disclose the material conflict arising from the significantly higher commission on the replacement product.

QUESTION
Under NY Insurance Regulation 187, did the producer satisfy the best interest standard when recommending the annuity replacement?

ANSWER
No, this conduct violates NY Insurance Regulation 187's best interest and disclosure requirements for annuity transactions.

Reg 187 requires that any recommendation to purchase or replace an annuity contract issued or delivered in New York must be in the consumer's best interest at the time of the transaction. The regulation mandates that the producer must document the basis for the recommendation, including why a replacement is superior to the existing product. Additionally, Reg 187 requires disclosure of material conflicts of interest, including compensation differentials. Here, the producer failed to document a best-interest analysis comparing the existing annuity to the replacement, failed to disclose the significant commission differential constituting a material conflict, and recommended a product with a 10-year surrender period and high surrender charges to a 72-year-old client who needs liquidity for healthcare—factors that are facially inconsistent with the client's stated objectives.

HYPOTHETICAL 662 | NON-COMPLIANT | 09_Law_Firm_Memos

FACTS
Apex Capital Partners, an SEC-registered investment adviser managing $2.1 billion across several private funds, grants one large institutional investor — a state pension fund committing $400 million — a side letter providing preferential redemption rights that allow full liquidity within 10 business days during a market dislocation event. The side letter was executed in March 2024, after the compliance date for the SEC's Preferential Treatment Rule under the Private Fund Adviser Rules. The adviser's chief compliance officer reviewed the letter but concluded that because the pension fund was a 'cornerstone investor,' no disclosure was required.

QUESTION
Did the registered investment adviser violate the SEC's Private Fund Adviser Rules by failing to disclose the preferential redemption terms granted via side letter to other investors in the same fund?

ANSWER

Preferential liquidity terms are specifically identified as material economic terms requiring written disclosure. The CCO's rationale that 'cornerstone investor' status exempts the adviser from disclosure has no basis in the rule; no such exception exists. The adviser's failure to provide notice to other LPs of the side letter's material terms constitutes a clear violation.

HYPOTHETICAL 677 | NON-COMPLIANT | 09_Law_Firm_Memos
============================================================

FACTS
Apex Capital Management is a SEC-registered investment adviser that manages three private funds with a combined $1.8 billion in AUM. In its most recent fund, Apex Fund III, the adviser granted preferential redemption rights to a $200 million institutional investor through a side letter, allowing quarterly redemptions while all other LPs are subject to a two-year lock-up. Apex did not disclose the existence or material terms of this preferential treatment to any other investors in Fund III, reasoning that the side letter was confidential and that the institutional investor's size justified differential treatment. The fund's PPM contained only generic language stating that 'the Adviser may enter into side arrangements with certain investors.' The preferential redemption right could materially disadvantage other LPs during a liquidity stress event by depleting fund assets before other investors can redeem.

QUESTION
Did Apex Capital Management comply with the SEC's Private Fund Adviser Rules regarding preferential treatment of investors through side letters?

ANSWER
No, this conduct violates the SEC's Preferential Treatment Rule under the Private Fund Adviser Rules.

Under the SEC's Private Fund Adviser Rules, preferential treatment regarding redemption rights that has a material negative effect on other investors is subject to specific disclosure requirements. The rule requires that advisers provide written notice to current and prospective investors detailing the material terms of any preferential treatment relating to redemptions or portfolio information. Generic PPM language referencing the possibility of 'side arrangements' is insufficient to satisfy the rule's disclosure obligations. Apex's failure to disclose the specific material terms of the preferential redemption right to other Fund III investors violates the preferential treatment disclosure provisions.

HYPOTHETICAL 678 | NON-COMPLIANT | 09_Law_Firm_Memos
============================================================

FACTS
A broker-dealer registered representative recommends that Maria Gonzalez, a 72-year-old retired schoolteacher with $340,000 in savings, a moderate risk tolerance, and a need for income stability, invest $280,000 in long-dated municipal revenue bonds rated BBB- with 25-year maturities. The representative earns a 2.8% markup on municipal bond transactions, significantly higher than the firm's average 1.1% markup on comparable fixed-income products. The representative did not evaluate alternative shorter-duration, higher-rated municipal bonds or other income-producing investments, nor did he document any analysis of why these particular bonds were preferable given the client's age, income needs, and risk profile. The firm's supervisory system flagged the markup as elevated but the branch manager approved the trade without additional review.

QUESTION
Did the broker-dealer representative satisfy the Care Obligation under Regulation Best Interest when recommending the long-dated, lower-rated municipal bonds to this retired client?

ANSWER
No, this conduct violates SEC Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii) – Reg BI Care Obligation.

The Care Obligation under Reg BI requires the representative to exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill in making a recommendation, including understanding the potential risks, rewards, and costs of the recommendation and having a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation is in the customer's best interest. Recommending 25-year maturity BBB- bonds to a 72-year-old retiree with moderate risk tolerance—without evaluating shorter-duration, higher-quality alternatives—fails to demonstrate reasonable diligence. The elevated markup further compounds the failure by imposing costs that were not weighed against the client's best interest. The MSRB's proposed alignment of Rule G-19 with Reg BI, as described in SR-MSRB-2020-02, reinforces that municipal securities recommendations must meet the same best interest standard.

HYPOTHETICAL 679 | COMPLIANT | 09_Law_Firm_Memos
============================================================

FACTS
Ridgeline Wealth Advisors, a dually registered investment adviser and broker-dealer, recommends that James Chen, a 55-year-old corporate executive with $2.1 million in investable assets and a growth-oriented risk profile, roll over $850,000 from his employer's 401(k) plan into a fee-based advisory IRA account. The adviser delivers a written rollover recommendation summary to Chen and maintains the analysis in the client file. QUESTION
Does the adviser's recommendation to roll over the 401(k) to a higher-cost advisory IRA comply with the SEC's investment adviser duty of care and Reg BI standards?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

The SEC's 2019 Fiduciary Interpretation articulates that the duty of care requires an adviser to provide advice in the best interest of the client, including a reasonable investigation into the costs and benefits of a recommendation such as a rollover. Here, the adviser conducted and documented a thorough comparative analysis weighing the higher cost against specific, quantifiable benefits (tax-loss harvesting alpha, alternative asset access, holistic planning) tailored to Chen's individual circumstances. The written rollover recommendation summary and compliance pre-approval demonstrate the kind of reasonable inquiry and documentation the SEC expects. Even if the SEC Staff Bulletins on standards of conduct are withdrawn as contemplated in reform proposals, the underlying duty of care under Section 206 of the Advisers Act remains operative.

HYPOTHETICAL 680 | NON-COMPLIANT | 09_Law_Firm_Memos
============================================================

FACTS
Greenfield Advisors LLC is an SEC-registered investment adviser managing $600 million across two private credit funds. The adviser charges a 1.5% management fee and a 20% performance allocation. Additionally, Greenfield allocates $1.2 million in broken-deal expenses from a failed acquisition across both funds on a pro-rata AUM basis, despite the fact that only Fund I was pursuing the acquisition. Fund II's LPA does not authorize the allocation of expenses from transactions not undertaken for Fund II's benefit. Greenfield does not disclose the allocation methodology or the fact that Fund II bore costs from Fund I's failed transaction.

QUESTION
Does Greenfield Advisors' expense allocation and financial reporting comply with the SEC's Private Fund Adviser Rules and the investment adviser's fiduciary duty?

ANSWER
No, this conduct violates the SEC Private Fund Adviser Rules and the investment adviser's fiduciary duty under Section 206 of the Advisers Act.

The Private Fund Adviser Rules require registered advisers to obtain annual financial statement audits for each private fund, making internally prepared quarterly statements an insufficient substitute. Additionally, the Restricted Activities Rule addresses the allocation of fees and expenses, requiring disclosure and, in certain cases, investor consent for expense allocations that may create conflicts. Allocating $1.2 million in broken-deal costs to Fund II—which had no involvement in the failed transaction and whose LPA did not authorize such allocation—constitutes a breach of fiduciary duty under Section 206 and violates the restricted activities provisions. The lack of disclosure compounds the violation.

Concentrating 78% of a retired couple's assets in a single illiquid, non-traded REIT with a 7-year holding period directly contradicts their stated need for potential liquidity and capital preservation. The 2025 State of Retirement Planning research shows that retirees who feel retirement is going 'as planned' rely on diversified, accessible portfolios—this recommendation undermines that outcome. The 7% commission creates a clear incentive conflict that was not mitigated by any documented analysis of alternatives.

The Conflict of Interest Obligation is addressed by the firm's compensation structure that does not preferentially incentivize the recommended products. Here, the adviser disclosed the affiliate relationship in Form ADV, provided a transaction-specific supplemental conflict disclosure, documented a comparative analysis showing the affiliated fund's superior risk-adjusted performance and below-median fees, and obtained informed written consent after a reasonable review period. HYPOTHETICAL 702 | NON-COMPLIANT | 09_Law_Firm_Memos
============================================================

FACTS
Greenfield Capital Advisors, an SEC-registered investment adviser with $850 million in AUM, has 14 supervised persons including 8 portfolio managers and 6 research analysts. In 2023, the firm updated its compliance manual to include general references to 'acting with integrity' and 'putting clients first,' but never adopted a formal, written code of ethics as a standalone document. The firm's CCO verbally instructed advisory personnel to avoid front-running client trades, but no written policies addressed personal securities trading, reporting of personal holdings, or pre-clearance of transactions. During a routine SEC examination, it was discovered that two portfolio managers had been actively trading the same small-cap equities in their personal accounts that they were simultaneously recommending to clients in the firm's wrap fee program, similar in structure to the Merrill Lynch Investment Advisory Program. Neither portfolio manager had ever reported personal securities transactions or initial/annual holdings to the firm.

QUESTION
Did Greenfield Capital Advisors comply with SEC requirements by relying on verbal instructions and general compliance manual language in lieu of a formal written code of ethics with personal trading provisions?

ANSWER

Rule 204A-1, adopted by the SEC on July 2, 2004, requires all SEC-registered investment advisers to establish, maintain, and enforce a written code of ethics that, at a minimum, includes standards of business conduct expected of supervised persons reflecting the adviser's fiduciary duties. The rule further requires that advisory personnel report personal securities holdings and transactions to enable detection of conflicts of interest such as front-running. Greenfield's reliance on verbal guidance and generic compliance manual language fails to satisfy these minimum requirements, and the absence of any personal trading reporting or pre-clearance procedures is a direct violation of the rule's personal trading provisions.

HYPOTHETICAL 703 | COMPLIANT | 09_Law_Firm_Memos
============================================================

FACTS
Cascade Benefits Group serves as a third-party administrator for a large ERISA-governed 401(k) plan with 12,000 participants sponsored by a Fortune 500 technology company. In June 2021, after the DOL published its final rule on e-delivery of retirement plan notices (effective May 27, 2020), Cascade transitioned to electronic delivery as the default method for all required DOL disclosures — including summary plan descriptions, quarterly benefit statements, and summary annual reports — for the 9,800 participants who had employer-provided email addresses and regular work computer access. For the remaining 2,200 participants who lacked consistent internet access (primarily field technicians), Cascade continued to send paper notices by first-class mail. Cascade's system sent an initial notification to each e-delivery participant explaining that disclosures would be provided electronically, included a free paper-copy request mechanism, and sent annual reminders of the right to opt out and receive paper. The system also monitored for invalid email addresses and bounced messages, reverting to paper delivery when electronic delivery failed.

QUESTION
Did Cascade Benefits Group comply with ERISA disclosure requirements by using e-delivery as the default method for plan participants with employer email addresses while maintaining paper delivery for those without internet access?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

The DOL's 2020 final rule on e-delivery established a safe harbor that permits electronic delivery as the permissible default method for DOL-required disclosures under ERISA, provided certain conditions are met. Cascade satisfied these conditions by limiting e-delivery to participants with employer-provided email addresses and regular computer access, providing initial and annual notices of the right to opt out and receive paper copies at no cost, monitoring for delivery failures and reverting to paper when necessary, and maintaining paper delivery for participants who lacked internet access. These measures collectively satisfy the safe harbor's requirements for covered individuals, notice, opt-out rights, and system safeguards.

HYPOTHETICAL 704 | NON-COMPLIANT | 10_Academic_Articles
============================================================

FACTS
Marcus Devlin, a registered representative with a FINRA member firm, accumulated three customer complaints and one regulatory action over a five-year period involving unsuitable variable annuity sales to elderly clients totaling $1.2 million in losses. Following a Form U5 filing disclosing these events, Devlin's broker-dealer terminated him. Rather than seeking employment with another FINRA-registered firm—where his CRD record would be visible to prospective employers and clients—Devlin obtained a state insurance license and began operating as an independent insurance agent selling equity-indexed annuities with 12-year surrender periods and 8% first-year commissions. He targeted the same demographic of retirees aged 68-82 with moderate fixed-income portfolios of $200,000-$500,000, recommending they liquidate existing bond holdings and CDs to purchase these products. Devlin did not disclose his prior misconduct history to any of his new insurance clients, and the state insurance regulator did not require him to do so.

QUESTION
Does Devlin's migration from the federal broker-dealer regime to state insurance regulation to continue selling functionally similar financial products to vulnerable retirees, while evading the disclosure and supervisory requirements that would apply under federal securities law, constitute a regulatory arbitrage pattern that violates investor protection principles under Reg BI and the securities laws?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is a regulatory arbitrage violation that circumvents Reg BI's Care and Disclosure Obligations and undermines the investor protection framework of the federal securities laws.

As documented in Honigsberg, Hu & Jackson (2022), advisors with serious misconduct records disproportionately exit the federal regulatory regime and continue advising investors under state insurance licenses, exploiting the 'light touch' of state insurance oversight. Devlin's conduct exemplifies this pattern: his CRD misconduct history—three complaints and a regulatory action—would trigger enhanced supervision or bar him from employment at a compliant broker-dealer under Reg BI's Compliance Obligation, yet he continues selling economically equivalent products (equity-indexed annuities versus variable annuities) to the same vulnerable client demographic. The 12-year surrender periods and high first-year commissions on products sold to clients aged 68-82 would independently fail Reg BI's Care Obligation requirement to consider reasonably available alternatives and act without placing the advisor's interest ahead of the client's. The failure to disclose his misconduct history violates the spirit of Reg BI's Disclosure Obligation, even though technically he has moved outside its jurisdictional reach.

HYPOTHETICAL 708 | COMPLIANT | 11_Case_Law
============================================================

FACTS
Bridgewater University sponsors a defined contribution 403(b) retirement plan with $1.2 billion in assets and 8,400 participants. The plan committee conducts a comprehensive review of its investment lineup every three years, with interim monitoring quarterly. During its 2023 triennial review, the committee evaluates the plan's suite of 22 investment options, including three target-date fund series. The committee identifies that the Vanguard Institutional Target Retirement funds have expense ratios approximately 3-5 basis points lower than the currently offered Fidelity Freedom Index funds. After deliberation documented in detailed meeting minutes, the committee retains the Fidelity funds, citing Fidelity's superior participant education platform, integrated recordkeeping efficiencies that reduce per-participant administrative costs by $18 annually, and comparable net-of-fee historical performance. A participant sues, alleging the committee breached its ERISA fiduciary duty by failing to select the lowest-cost option.

QUESTION
Did the plan committee breach its ERISA fiduciary duty of prudence by retaining slightly higher-cost target-date funds when a marginally cheaper alternative existed?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

Under Hughes v. Northwestern, fiduciaries have a duty to monitor investments and cannot simply rely on offering a broad menu. However, the duty of prudence under ERISA is a process-based standard, not an outcome-based one. The committee satisfied Tibble's ongoing monitoring requirement through quarterly reviews and triennial comprehensive evaluations. The documented deliberation—weighing expense ratios against participant education benefits, administrative cost savings, and net-of-fee performance—demonstrates the kind of reasoned, informed process that courts evaluate. A 3-5 basis point difference offset by $18 per-participant administrative savings and comparable performance reflects a prudent fiduciary judgment, not a breach.

HYPOTHETICAL 710 | COMPLIANT | 11_Case_Law
============================================================

FACTS
Apex Capital Management, an SEC-registered investment adviser with $890 million in AUM, holds a 10.3% beneficial ownership stake in Cortland Industries (NASDAQ: CRTD) across multiple client accounts. After accumulating this position over 14 months, Apex files a Schedule 13D within 10 days of crossing the 10% threshold as required. Three weeks later, Cortland's stock rises 18% following a positive earnings surprise, and Apex sells 2.1% of the position across client accounts to rebalance portfolios, reducing its stake to 8.2%. The entire holding period from crossing 10% to the partial sale spans approximately 33 days. A Cortland shareholder files a derivative Section 16(b) short-swing profit claim against Apex, seeking disgorgement of profits on the theory that Apex was a 10% beneficial owner at the time of the sale.

QUESTION
Is Apex Capital Management's sale of Cortland Industries shares within six months of crossing the 10% beneficial ownership threshold a Section 16(b) short-swing profit violation requiring disgorgement?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

Section 16(b) requires that a person be a 10% beneficial owner both at the time of the purchase and at the time of the sale for the short-swing profit provision to apply. As analyzed in the Packer v. Raging Capital framework, the critical question is whether the purchase that brought Apex above 10% and the subsequent sale both occurred while Apex was a statutory insider. Here, Apex properly filed its Schedule 13D, and the purchase that crossed the 10% threshold was not itself subject to Section 16(b) liability because the purchaser was not yet a 10% owner at the time of that crossing purchase. The subsequent sale, while Apex was above 10%, can only be matched with purchases made after Apex became a 10% owner, limiting the scope of any potential disgorgement to profits on shares purchased after the threshold was crossed, which in this case were not part of the sale.

HYPOTHETICAL 711 | NON-COMPLIANT | 11_Case_Law
============================================================

FACTS
GlobalRetire Services, a non-fiduciary third-party administrator, contracts with 47 employer-sponsored 401(k) plans to offer participant loan programs. Under the program, participants can borrow up to 50% of their vested balance, secured by their retirement savings. GlobalRetire charges a $150 loan origination fee plus an annual servicing fee of 1.25% of the outstanding loan balance — both paid from participant accounts — significantly exceeding market rates for comparable loan administration services. The plan fiduciaries who contracted with GlobalRetire did not solicit competitive bids or benchmark GlobalRetire's fees against other providers. GlobalRetire also retains the spread between the interest rate participants pay (prime + 3%) and the rate credited back to participant accounts (prime + 1%), generating $4.2 million annually across all plans. No plan document or summary plan description discloses the interest rate spread retained by GlobalRetire.

QUESTION
Does GlobalRetire's participant loan program structure constitute a prohibited transaction under ERISA, even though GlobalRetire is a non-fiduciary service provider?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is a prohibited transaction under ERISA Section 406(a).

Under ERISA § 406(a)(1)(C) and (D), a transaction involving plan assets that furnishes goods, services, or facilities between a plan and a party in interest, or that transfers plan assets to a party in interest, may constitute a prohibited transaction regardless of whether the service provider is itself a fiduciary. As the Second Circuit held in Haley v. TIAA, a non-fiduciary can be sued under ERISA where the loan program it administers constitutes a prohibited transaction. The undisclosed retention of the interest rate spread and the above-market fees extracted from participant accounts without competitive benchmarking by plan fiduciaries compound the violation. The plan fiduciaries' failure to solicit competitive bids also implicates their own duty of prudence under ERISA § 404(a)(1)(B).

HYPOTHETICAL 712 | NON-COMPLIANT | 11_Case_Law
============================================================

FACTS
Ridgeline Capital Advisors, a registered investment adviser managing $320 million in client assets, maintains a revenue-sharing arrangement with Apex Clearing Corporation under which Ridgeline receives 15 basis points annually on client assets custodied at Apex. Ridgeline's Form ADV Part 2A includes a general statement that the firm 'may receive compensation from third parties in connection with custody and clearing services.' However, the disclosure does not identify Apex by name, does not quantify the revenue-sharing payments (which totaled $480,000 in the prior year), and does not explain that this arrangement creates an incentive for Ridgeline to custody client assets at Apex rather than at lower-cost alternatives. When the SEC staff inquired during an examination, Ridgeline's chief compliance officer stated the firm believed its generic disclosure was adequate.

QUESTION
Is Ridgeline's generic disclosure of its revenue-sharing arrangement with its custodian sufficient under the Investment Advisers Act's fiduciary duty of disclosure?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is a violation of the Investment Advisers Act fiduciary duty and SEC disclosure requirements.

Under Sections 206(1) and 206(2) of the Investment Advisers Act, an investment adviser has a fiduciary duty to make full and fair disclosure of all material conflicts of interest. In Robare Group v. SEC, the D.C. Circuit addressed whether an adviser's generic disclosure of a revenue-sharing arrangement was adequate, emphasizing the materiality of such conflicts and the need for specificity. Ridgeline's failure to identify the specific custodian, quantify the payments, or explain the resulting conflict means clients cannot assess whether Ridgeline's custodial recommendation is truly in their best interest. The $480,000 annual payment is material and creates a concrete incentive that must be disclosed with particularity.
