HYPOTHETICAL 713 | COMPLIANT | 11_Case_Law
============================================================

FACTS
Midwestern University sponsors a defined contribution retirement plan with $1.8 billion in assets and 12,000 participants. The plan's investment committee conducts a comprehensive review of all plan investment options every three years, supplemented by quarterly performance monitoring. During the 2023 triennial review, the committee evaluates the plan's existing suite of 22 mutual funds and discovers that three funds have institutional share classes available at lower expense ratios — ranging from 8 to 14 basis points lower — than the retail share classes currently offered. The committee documents its analysis, negotiates with the recordkeeper to transition to institutional shares, and completes the share class conversion within 90 days. A participant subsequently files suit alleging the committee breached its fiduciary duty by originally selecting and retaining the higher-cost retail share classes for approximately two years before converting, citing Tibble v. Edison International.

QUESTION
Did the university's investment committee satisfy its ongoing duty to monitor plan investments under ERISA despite initially offering higher-cost retail share classes?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

In Tibble v. Edison International, the Supreme Court held that ERISA fiduciaries have a continuing duty to monitor trust investments and remove imprudent ones within a reasonable time. However, this duty requires a prudent process, not a guarantee of the lowest-cost option at every moment. Here, the committee maintained a documented, systematic review process with quarterly monitoring and triennial comprehensive reviews. Upon discovering the availability of lower-cost institutional share classes, the committee acted promptly — completing the transition within 90 days. The two-year period during which retail shares were offered is defensible because the committee's monitoring process was reasonable and the fiduciaries acted within a reasonable time after discovering the issue.

HYPOTHETICAL 714 | NON-COMPLIANT | 11_Case_Law
============================================================

FACTS
Martin Greystone is the sole portfolio manager at Greystone Wealth Management, a registered investment adviser. Greystone personally acquires a 12% equity stake in a publicly traded company, NovaTech Inc. (market cap $180 million), making him a beneficial owner of more than 10% of NovaTech's outstanding shares. Over the following four months, Greystone sells his entire NovaTech position at a substantial profit of $2.3 million. During this same period, Greystone allocates NovaTech shares to seven client accounts without disclosing his personal ownership stake or his active trading in the same security. None of the clients are informed that their adviser is simultaneously unwinding a large personal position in the same stock.

QUESTION
Did Greystone violate his fiduciary obligations and securities law by trading NovaTech shares in client accounts while simultaneously liquidating his own 10%-plus position without disclosure?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is a violation of the Investment Advisers Act fiduciary duty and Section 16(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.

As a 10% beneficial owner under Section 16(b) of the Exchange Act, Greystone's purchase and sale of NovaTech shares within a six-month window subjects him to short-swing profit disgorgement requirements, as the Second Circuit analyzed in Packer v. Raging Capital Management. Additionally, under Advisers Act §§ 206(1) and 206(2), Greystone has a fiduciary duty to disclose material conflicts of interest to clients, including his personal ownership of and trading in the same securities he allocates to client accounts. The failure to disclose his 12% stake and concurrent liquidation constitutes a material omission and a breach of the duty of loyalty.

HYPOTHETICAL 715 | COMPLIANT | 11_Case_Law
============================================================

FACTS
Lakeview Regional Hospital sponsors a 403(b) retirement plan with $240 million in assets for its 3,400 employees. The plan offers a diversified menu of 18 investment options across asset classes, including a suite of low-cost index funds from Vanguard and Fidelity with expense ratios ranging from 0.03% to 0.15%, as well as four actively managed funds with expense ratios between 0.55% and 0.82%. The plan's investment committee, composed of five hospital administrators with investment experience, meets quarterly to review each fund's performance, fees, and peer-group comparisons. Committee meeting minutes document that the actively managed funds were retained because they provided exposure to asset classes (such as emerging market debt and real assets) not readily available through low-cost index alternatives, and because the committee determined participants valued having both passive and active options. A participant files suit under ERISA alleging the committee breached its duty of prudence by offering any funds with expense ratios above 0.20%, citing Hughes v. Northwestern University.

QUESTION
Did the plan investment committee breach its ERISA fiduciary duty by retaining actively managed funds with higher expense ratios alongside low-cost index options?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

In Hughes v. Northwestern University, the Supreme Court held that even when a plan offers some low-cost options, fiduciaries are not automatically insulated from claims that other options are imprudent. However, the Court's holding does not prohibit offering actively managed funds; rather, it requires that fiduciaries engage in a prudent process when selecting and monitoring all investment options. Here, the Lakeview committee maintained a documented quarterly review process, evaluated each fund against peer benchmarks, and articulated a specific investment rationale for retaining the actively managed funds — namely, they provide diversified asset class exposure not available through index options. The deliberate, well-documented decision-making process satisfies the procedural prudence standard under ERISA § 404(a)(1)(B).

HYPOTHETICAL 716 | NON-COMPLIANT | 11_Case_Law
============================================================

FACTS
GreenLeaf Retirement Services administers a 403(b) plan for a large university system with 12,000 participants and $1.8 billion in assets. GreenLeaf offers a participant loan program where loans are secured by the participant's retirement savings. The loan interest rates are set at prime plus 3%, significantly above the market rate for comparable secured loans, and GreenLeaf retains the interest rate spread as additional compensation beyond its stated administrative fees. The plan fiduciaries approved the loan program without conducting any analysis of whether the loan terms were reasonable compared to market alternatives, and the plan document does not specifically authorize GreenLeaf to retain the interest spread. A participant who borrowed $45,000 against her account paid $8,200 in excess interest over the loan term compared to what she would have paid at prevailing market rates for similar secured credit.

QUESTION
Does GreenLeaf's participant loan program, where the service provider retains above-market interest spreads as undisclosed additional compensation, comply with ERISA's prohibited transaction rules?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is a prohibited transaction under ERISA § 406(a)(1)(D) involving the use of plan assets for the benefit of a party in interest, and potentially a violation of § 406(b) if GreenLeaf is deemed a fiduciary.

As analyzed in Haley v. TIAA, a participant loan program offered by a service provider can constitute a prohibited transaction under ERISA when the service provider uses plan assets (the participant's retirement savings securing the loan) to generate compensation that exceeds reasonable amounts. Under ERISA § 408(b)(2), a loan program is exempt from prohibited transaction rules only if the compensation is reasonable and the arrangement is disclosed. GreenLeaf's retention of an above-market interest spread without disclosure or fiduciary approval of that specific compensation component fails the statutory exemption requirements. The Second Circuit's holding that such claims can proceed against non-fiduciary service providers under ERISA § 502(a)(3) further underscores that the conduct is actionable.

HYPOTHETICAL 717 | NON-COMPLIANT | 11_Case_Law
============================================================

FACTS
Meridian Capital Advisors, a registered investment adviser managing $340 million in client assets, has a revenue-sharing arrangement with Pinnacle Mutual Funds whereby Meridian receives 15 basis points on all client assets directed into Pinnacle products. Meridian's Form ADV Part 2A states that 'the firm may receive compensation from third-party fund companies,' but does not identify Pinnacle by name, quantify the revenue-sharing amount, or explain how this creates a financial incentive to recommend Pinnacle funds over lower-cost alternatives. Over the past three years, 72% of client assets have been placed in Pinnacle funds, despite several comparable index funds from other providers carrying expense ratios 30-45 basis points lower. When examined by the SEC, Meridian's chief compliance officer stated the firm believed its generic ADV disclosure was sufficient.

QUESTION
Does Meridian's generic disclosure of potential third-party compensation in its Form ADV satisfy the Investment Advisers Act's fiduciary duty to disclose material conflicts of interest?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is a violation of the Investment Advisers Act §§ 206(1) and 206(2) for failure to adequately disclose material conflicts of interest.

In Robare Group v. SEC, the D.C. Circuit addressed the adequacy of conflict disclosures involving revenue-sharing arrangements. While the court scrutinized the SEC's scienter findings, it affirmed the principle that an investment adviser's fiduciary duty under §§ 206(1) and 206(2) requires disclosure that is sufficiently specific to allow clients to understand the nature, magnitude, and implications of the conflict. A generic statement that the firm 'may receive compensation' without identifying the specific fund family, the amount of compensation, or the resulting incentive to favor those products over cheaper alternatives fails to provide the informed consent that fiduciary duty requires. Meridian's 72% concentration in higher-cost Pinnacle funds while receiving undisclosed basis-point payments demonstrates the materiality of the conflict.

HYPOTHETICAL 718 | COMPLIANT | 11_Case_Law
============================================================

FACTS
Apex University sponsors a defined contribution 403(b) plan with $2.1 billion in assets and 8,500 participants. The plan's investment committee conducts a comprehensive review of its investment lineup every 18 months, engaging an independent investment consultant to benchmark all funds against peer groups for performance, expense ratios, and risk-adjusted returns. During the 2023 review, the committee identified that three actively managed large-cap equity funds had expense ratios of 62-78 basis points, compared to an available S&P 500 index fund charging 3 basis points. After deliberation documented in detailed meeting minutes, the committee decided to retain two of the three active funds based on evidence of consistent alpha generation over 10-year periods and the consultant's recommendation, while replacing the third with the index option. A plan participant files an ERISA breach-of-fiduciary-duty complaint alleging the committee should have replaced all actively managed options with index funds.

QUESTION
Does the plan investment committee's decision to retain actively managed funds with higher expense ratios, after a documented prudent review process, constitute a breach of fiduciary duty under ERISA?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

While Hughes v. Northwestern held that ERISA fiduciaries cannot escape judicial scrutiny simply by offering a wide range of options, and Tibble established a continuing duty to monitor plan investments, neither case mandates that fiduciaries must select the lowest-cost option available. The ERISA prudent man standard under § 404(a)(1)(B) requires a prudent process, not a particular outcome. Here, the committee engaged an independent consultant, conducted regular benchmarking reviews, documented its analysis and rationale, and actually removed one underperforming fund — demonstrating the type of ongoing, deliberate monitoring that Tibble requires. The decision to retain funds with demonstrated long-term alpha generation, supported by expert analysis, reflects the procedural prudence that courts evaluate.

HYPOTHETICAL 719 | COMPLIANT | 11_Case_Law
============================================================

FACTS
Clearwater Advisory Group, an SEC-registered investment adviser with $520 million under management, allocates certain client accounts into a private real estate fund managed by a separate entity in which Clearwater's founder holds a 12% limited partnership interest. Clearwater's Form ADV Part 2A specifically identifies the private fund by name, discloses the founder's 12% ownership stake, states the exact management and incentive fees charged by the fund (1.5% management fee and 20% carried interest above an 8% hurdle), explains that the founder benefits financially when client assets are allocated to the fund, and quantifies the estimated annual economic benefit to the founder at approximately $185,000. Each affected client receives a separate written conflict disclosure and signs an informed consent acknowledgment before any allocation is made. Clearwater's compliance department maintains a log of all consents and reviews each allocation for investment suitability relative to the client's stated objectives and risk tolerance.

QUESTION
Does Clearwater's allocation of client assets to a private fund in which its founder has a financial interest comply with the Investment Advisers Act's fiduciary duty requirements?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

The Investment Advisers Act's fiduciary duty, as articulated in Capital Gains Research Bureau and interpreted in Robare Group, requires full and fair disclosure of material conflicts of interest sufficient to obtain informed client consent. Unlike the deficient generic disclosures at issue in Robare Group, Clearwater provides specific, quantified disclosure identifying the exact fund, the founder's precise ownership percentage, the fee structure, the estimated dollar benefit to the founder, and the nature of the conflict. Each client provides individualized written informed consent, and the firm independently evaluates suitability. This level of specificity and process represents the type of disclosure that satisfies the adviser's fiduciary obligations.

HYPOTHETICAL 720 | NON-COMPLIANT | 11_Case_Law

FACTS
Marcus Webb, a registered representative at Summit Securities, recommends that his client, 71-year-old retired schoolteacher Dorothy Hanson, invest $320,000 — representing approximately 85% of her liquid retirement savings — into a non-traded REIT with a 7-year lockup period, 12% upfront commission, and no secondary market liquidity. Mrs. Hanson's account documents indicate a conservative risk tolerance, a need for income to supplement her $1,400 monthly pension, and potential need for funds to cover assisted living costs within three to five years. Webb's rationale documented in his recommendation notes states only that 'client wants higher yield than CDs.' Summit Securities' compliance department approved the transaction through an automated system that flagged no alerts because the product was on the firm's approved list.

Does Marcus Webb's recommendation of a non-traded REIT with a 7-year lockup to a 71-year-old retiree who may need liquidity within 3-5 years comply with Regulation Best Interest?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is a violation of Regulation Best Interest's Care Obligation and the firm's Compliance Obligation.

Reg BI's Care Obligation requires a broker-dealer to exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill in making recommendations, considering the investment's risks, rewards, and costs in light of the specific customer's investment profile including age, liquidity needs, risk tolerance, and time horizon. Recommending an illiquid product with a 7-year lockup and 12% upfront load to a 71-year-old conservative investor who may need funds within 3-5 years for assisted living directly contradicts her documented investment profile. The firm's Compliance Obligation is also implicated because Summit's automated approval system failed to flag obvious red flags — concentration of 85% of liquid assets in a single illiquid product for an elderly, conservative client — indicating inadequate policies and procedures to achieve compliance with Reg BI.

HYPOTHETICAL 721 | NON-COMPLIANT | 11_Case_Law

FACTS

GlobalRetire retains the interest rate spread as additional compensation beyond its stated administrative fees, but the loan program terms are buried in a 200-page service agreement that plan fiduciaries did not independently negotiate. QUESTION
Does GlobalRetire's operation of the participant loan program, where it retains above-market interest as undisclosed additional compensation, constitute a prohibited transaction under ERISA?

HYPOTHETICAL 722 | NON-COMPLIANT | 11_Case_Law

FACTS
Harron Capital Advisors, a registered investment adviser, is co-managing an international real estate fund alongside its principals' personal investment vehicle. Harron's personal vehicle co-invests in the same properties but receives a disproportionately favorable allocation of the most profitable assets, while the fund managed on behalf of outside investors receives the lower-performing properties. The fund's PPM discloses that 'affiliates may co-invest alongside the fund' but does not disclose the specific allocation methodology or the conflict inherent in Harron's dual role in setting valuations. Does the investment adviser's failure to disclose the specific conflict of interest in asset allocation between the fund and the principal's personal vehicle violate the Investment Advisers Act?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is a violation of the Investment Advisers Act's anti-fraud provisions and fiduciary duty of loyalty.

Under the Investment Advisers Act, an investment adviser owes a fiduciary duty that requires full and fair disclosure of all material conflicts of interest. As illustrated in the Metro Storage v. Harron pattern, where a co-venturer engaged in self-dealing allocation of business opportunities, a generic disclosure that 'affiliates may co-invest' is insufficient when the adviser is actively directing the most favorable assets to its own account. The Robare Group decision further underscores that the SEC requires specificity in conflict disclosures—boilerplate language does not satisfy the adviser's duty to ensure clients can provide informed consent.

HYPOTHETICAL 723 | COMPLIANT | 11_Case_Law

FACTS
Beacon Retirement Services serves as the investment committee for a university's $2.1 billion 403(b) defined contribution plan with 28,000 participants. The plan offers a lineup of 42 investment options, including several institutional share class mutual funds with expense ratios ranging from 0.03% to 0.72%. An internal audit reveals that three actively managed funds have underperformed their benchmarks for three consecutive years. ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

Under Tibble v. Edison, ERISA fiduciaries have a continuing duty to monitor plan investments and remove imprudent ones. However, this duty requires a prudent process, not a specific outcome. Here, the investment committee engaged in a well-documented, deliberative process including quarterly reviews, engagement of an independent consultant, substantive analysis of the reasons for underperformance, and active negotiation of lower fees. Hughes v. Northwestern reinforced that fiduciaries must engage in ongoing monitoring but did not mandate automatic removal upon underperformance. The documented, reasoned decision to retain funds during a monitoring period—supported by independent analysis—satisfies the procedural prudence standard.

HYPOTHETICAL 725 | COMPLIANT | 11_Case_Law

FACTS
Ridgeline Wealth Management, a fee-only registered investment adviser, manages approximately $380 million in client assets. (NXTR), and receives $45,000 annually in board compensation plus restricted stock units. Additionally, Ridgeline delivers a separate written conflict disclosure to every client at account opening and annually thereafter, specifically identifying Paulson's board role and the firm's resulting trading restriction. Does the investment adviser's CIO serving on a public company board create an impermissible conflict of interest under the Investment Advisers Act?

HYPOTHETICAL 726 | NON-COMPLIANT | 12_FINRA_Arbitration_Awards
============================================================

FACTS
Fortune Financial Services, a FINRA member firm headquartered in Monaca, Pennsylvania with approximately 280 registered representatives across 200 branch offices, failed to establish adequate written supervisory procedures for the sale of deferred variable annuities from July 2016 through July 2021. During this period, registered representative Mark Hollis recommended that 74-year-old retired schoolteacher Doris Engel exchange her existing deferred variable annuity—which had passed its surrender period—into a new deferred variable annuity with an 8-year surrender schedule and higher annual fees of 3.45% versus 2.10%, without documenting any material benefit to the client. Doris filed a FINRA arbitration claim alleging unsuitable recommendations and failure to supervise, seeking $87,000 in damages representing excess costs and surrender charges.

QUESTION
Did the firm's failure to maintain written supervisory procedures requiring principal review and cost-benefit comparison of variable annuity exchanges violate its supervisory obligations?

ANSWER

FINRA Rule 2330 specifically requires that a registered principal review and approve each deferred variable annuity exchange transaction, considering whether the customer would incur a surrender charge, lose existing benefits, or face a new surrender period. FINRA Rule 3110 mandates that firms establish and maintain a system to supervise activities of each registered representative reasonably designed to achieve compliance. A five-year gap in supervisory procedures for annuity exchanges, as paralleled in the Fortune Financial AWC, constitutes a systemic supervision failure.

The customer's failure to appear at the hearing further undermines the claim, as seen in Patten v. HYPOTHETICAL 728 | NON-COMPLIANT | 12_FINRA_Arbitration_Awards

FACTS

UBS (FINRA Case No. 16-03079), a customer's receipt of account statements does not constitute ratification of an unsuitable investment strategy, particularly where the advisor owes a fiduciary duty. The advisor's duty to recommend suitable investments is independent of the client's failure to object to account statements.

HYPOTHETICAL 729 | COMPLIANT | 12_FINRA_Arbitration_Awards

HYPOTHETICAL 730 | NON-COMPLIANT | 12_FINRA_Arbitration_Awards
============================================================

FACTS
Wells Fargo Clearing Services, LLC financial advisor Eric Koter managed the $1.4 million joint brokerage account of retired couple Gerald and Patricia Simmons, ages 71 and 68. Without obtaining prior written authorization for discretionary trading, Koter executed 214 trades over a 22-month period, generating $127,000 in commissions and an annualized turnover rate of 8.2. The account's stated investment objective was 'capital preservation and income,' and the couple's annual income need was $48,000. An annualized turnover rate of 8.2 far exceeds the threshold of 6.0 that FINRA and courts have consistently held to be presumptive evidence of churning, particularly in a capital preservation account. Under FINRA Rule 3260, a broker may not exercise discretionary authority without prior written authorization from the customer and acceptance of the account as discretionary by the firm. The execution of 214 trades without written discretionary authority constitutes unauthorized trading regardless of whether the client received statements. As reflected in cases involving Wells Fargo Clearing Services in FINRA proceedings, the availability of account statements does not constitute informed consent to excessive trading or relieve the firm of supervisory liability.

Fortune Financial Services, a FINRA member firm headquartered in Monaca, Pennsylvania with approximately 280 registered representatives across 200 branch offices, allowed multiple deferred variable annuity exchanges for elderly clients between July 2016 and July 2021 without adequate supervisory review. A 74-year-old retired schoolteacher, Margaret Downs, was switched from one deferred variable annuity to another three times in four years, each time incurring new surrender charges averaging $8,200 per exchange. The registered representative earned new commissions on each exchange totaling $14,500 while no meaningful change in investment features or riders benefited the client. The firm's written supervisory procedures did not require a documented cost-benefit analysis for variable annuity exchanges, and no principal reviewed whether the transactions were suitable.

QUESTION
Did the firm's failure to implement supervisory procedures requiring documented cost-benefit analyses for variable annuity exchanges violate its supervisory obligations?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is not compliant. The firm failed to establish and maintain a supervisory system reasonably designed to detect and prevent unsuitable variable annuity exchanges.

FINRA Rule 3110 requires member firms to establish and maintain written supervisory procedures reasonably designed to achieve compliance with applicable securities laws and regulations. The firm's failure to require any cost-benefit analysis for variable annuity exchanges—particularly for elderly clients vulnerable to surrender charge losses—mirrors the findings in the Fortune Financial Services AWC (No. 2020065435403), where the firm's supervisory system was found deficient from July 2016 through July 2021 regarding deferred variable annuity transactions. Serial exchanges generating new commissions without documented client benefit constitute a textbook supervisory failure.

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

A firm cannot guarantee that no representative will ever engage in misconduct; the supervisory obligation under FINRA Rules 3110 and 3120 requires that firms maintain reasonably designed systems to detect and respond to violations. Wells Fargo's exception-reporting surveillance system detected the unauthorized trading within 45 days, the firm promptly placed Koter on heightened supervision, terminated him within 90 days after completing its investigation, and voluntarily made customers whole before pursuing indemnification. This sequence demonstrates a supervisory system that functioned as designed—detecting misconduct, escalating appropriately, and remediating customer harm. The firm's subsequent petition to confirm the arbitration award against the former representative (consistent with the Wells Fargo v. Koter proceeding) further demonstrates accountability measures.

FACTS

HYPOTHETICAL 748 | NON-COMPLIANT | 13_FINRA_Rulebook

An internal audit reveals that Karen reviewed only 312 of these transactions, with average review times of under 90 seconds per transaction. Here, the batch electronic approval of 535 transactions without individualized substantive review fails Rule 2330's principal approval mandate. Sandra has a moderate-to-aggressive risk tolerance, a retirement time horizon of 5-7 years, $920,000 in total liquid assets, a pension income of $4,800/month, and no anticipated need for the annuity funds within the surrender period. James prepares a detailed written comparison documenting the surrender charge differential, the fee savings over the projected holding period, the additional rider benefits, and the tax implications of the exchange. The firm's designated principal, after reviewing the full comparison document, Sandra's updated investment profile, and the exchange rationale, approves the transaction three business days before it is processed, and documents her independent analysis in the firm's supervisory review log.

QUESTION
Does this recommended variable annuity exchange comply with the suitability, documentation, and principal review requirements of FINRA Rule 2330?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

FINRA Rule 2330 requires that an exchange recommendation be based on a reasonable belief that the transaction is suitable given the customer's age, liquidity needs, investment objectives, time horizon, existing benefits, and cost differentials. Here, the representative conducted and documented a thorough comparative analysis showing meaningful fee reduction, enhanced features, and suitability alignment with the client's profile — the client has ample liquidity, no near-term need for the funds, and a time horizon well beyond the new surrender period. Under Rule 2330(c), a registered principal reviewed and approved the transaction before processing, examining the full comparison, the client's updated profile, and the exchange rationale, and documented her independent assessment. This sequence satisfies the rule's substantive suitability, documentation, and prior-principal-approval requirements.

FACTS
A registered representative at a mid-sized broker-dealer recommends that Margaret Chen, a 78-year-old retired schoolteacher with $180,000 in liquid savings and a conservative risk tolerance, exchange her existing deferred variable annuity — which has exited its surrender period — for a new deferred variable annuity with a 7-year surrender schedule and an annual mortality and expense charge of 1.45%. The representative processes the exchange the same day the recommendation is made without forwarding the transaction to a registered principal for review. Did the representative and the firm comply with FINRA Rule 2330 requirements for the recommended deferred variable annuity exchange?

Recommending a new 7-year surrender period to a 78-year-old with no need for the income rider fails this test. Additionally, Rule 2330(c) mandates that a registered principal review and approve the transaction before the purchase or exchange is processed. HYPOTHETICAL 752 | NON-COMPLIANT | 13_FINRA_Rulebook
============================================================

FACTS
David Morales, a registered representative, recommends that Brian Kowalski, a 34-year-old software engineer earning $145,000 annually with moderate risk tolerance and a 5-year investment horizon for a home down payment, invest $95,000 — representing 85% of his liquid net worth — into a concentrated position in a single leveraged inverse ETF tracking the Nasdaq-100 index. David documents Brian's investment profile as required under FINRA Rule 2090 but does not perform any analysis of whether the leveraged inverse ETF is consistent with Brian's stated moderate risk tolerance and medium-term time horizon. The firm's suitability review checklist was completed by David himself with no independent supervisory review.

QUESTION
Does this recommendation satisfy the reasonable-basis and customer-specific suitability obligations under FINRA Rule 2111?

ANSWER
No, this conduct violates FINRA Rule 2111(a) — both the reasonable-basis and customer-specific suitability obligations.

Leveraged inverse ETFs are complex products designed for short-term trading and can produce returns dramatically different from their benchmark over holding periods longer than one day — making them inappropriate for a 5-year hold. Concentrating 85% of liquid net worth in such a product for a client with moderate risk tolerance and a specific savings goal violates customer-specific suitability. The representative's failure to perform any product-level analysis also fails the reasonable-basis obligation.

FINRA Rule 3110 requires member firms to establish, maintain, and enforce written supervisory procedures reasonably designed to achieve compliance with applicable rules. Greenfield's actual practice of threshold-based batch approvals directly contradicts its own written procedures requiring individualized review, demonstrating both a failure to follow and a failure to enforce its WSPs. HYPOTHETICAL 767 | NON-COMPLIANT | 14_NASAA_State_Enforcement
============================================================

FACTS
Kuber Wealth Partners, LLC, a state-registered investment adviser in Georgia with CRD No. 310882, managed approximately $28 million in assets for 74 clients. QUESTION
Did Kuber Wealth Partners violate NASAA Model Custody Rule 102(e)(1)-1 by failing to meet custody safekeeping requirements?

ANSWER

Under NASAA Model Rule 102(e)(1)-1(a), it is deemed a fraudulent, deceptive, or manipulative act for a registered investment adviser to have custody of client funds unless the adviser promptly notifies the administrator in writing via Form ADV, maintains funds with a qualified custodian in separate accounts under each client's name or in properly designated omnibus accounts, and complies with the surprise examination requirement. Kuber Wealth Partners failed on all three prongs. The unauthorized fee withdrawals from the retiree's account further evidence the risks the custody rule is designed to prevent.

HYPOTHETICAL 768 | NON-COMPLIANT | 14_NASAA_State_Enforcement
============================================================

FACTS
Crescent Digital Advisors, LLC, a Michigan state-registered investment adviser, marketed a proprietary 'Digital Asset Growth Fund' to retail clients, raising $3.2 million from 41 investors, most of whom were retirees and schoolteachers with moderate risk tolerances. The fund invested primarily in unregistered digital asset tokens that Crescent's principal described as 'investment contracts with guaranteed blockchain yields of 18% annually.' Crescent did not register the pooled investment vehicle's interests as securities with the State of Michigan, did not provide clients with audited financial statements, and commingled fund assets with the firm's operating account at a commercial bank rather than maintaining them with a qualified custodian. QUESTION
Did Crescent Digital Advisors violate state securities laws by offering unregistered securities, failing custody requirements, and operating a fraudulent scheme?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is not compliant. This constitutes multiple violations including offer and sale of unregistered securities, custody rule violations under NASAA Model Rule 102(e)(1)-1, and fraud under state anti-fraud provisions.

Crescent violated state law on multiple fronts. First, the interests in the Digital Asset Growth Fund constituted investment contracts under the Howey test—investors pooled money with an expectation of profits derived from Crescent's efforts—and were never registered with Michigan. Second, commingling fund assets with the firm's operating account violated the NASAA Model Custody Rule requiring a qualified custodian to hold client funds in segregated accounts. Third, paying existing investors with new investor money constitutes a Ponzi-like fraudulent scheme under state anti-fraud statutes. NASAA's coordinated examination initiative, which examined 1,086 advisers in 2025, is precisely designed to uncover these overlapping violations, especially among advisers being examined for the first time.

Yes, this conduct is compliant.

There is no minimum waiting period mandated beyond the DFPI's processing and approval of the application; once approved, the firm may lawfully begin advisory activities. The firm also properly disclosed custody on Form ADV, uses a qualified custodian (Charles Schwab) maintaining separate client accounts, and arranged for a surprise examination—satisfying all prongs of NASAA Model Rule 102(e)(1)-1(a). The speed of registration does not, by itself, indicate any deficiency.

Mehta has not notified the state administrator of having custody via Form ADV Item 9, has not engaged a qualified custodian to hold the assets in separate accounts for each client under the client's name, and has not arranged for an annual surprise examination. Mehta periodically transfers funds between the omnibus account and his firm's operating account to cover business expenses, later replenishing the amounts.

QUESTION
Does the firm's handling of client funds comply with the NASAA Model Custody Rule 102(e)(1)-1 and applicable state custody requirements?

ANSWER
No, this conduct constitutes multiple violations of NASAA Model Rule 102(e)(1)-1, including failure to notify the administrator of custody, failure to use a qualified custodian maintaining separate client accounts, and commingling client funds with firm operating funds.

Under NASAA Model Rule 102(e)(1)-1(a), it is deemed a fraudulent, deceptive, or manipulative act for a registered investment adviser to have custody of client funds unless the adviser (1) promptly notifies the administrator in writing via Form ADV, (2) uses a qualified custodian to maintain those funds in separate accounts for each client under the client's name or in accounts containing only clients' funds under the adviser's name as agent or trustee, and (3) provides required notice to clients. In total, investors in the offering effectively pay 10.05% in combined front-end and ongoing compensation to the firm over the first year, with the additional payments not disclosed in the manner required under FINRA's Corporate Financing Rules.

QUESTION
Did the firm comply with FINRA's Corporate Financing Rules by structuring distribution fees and marketing support payments outside of reported underwriting compensation?

ANSWER
No, this conduct violates FINRA's Corporate Financing Rules regarding underwriting compensation disclosure.

FINRA's Corporate Financing Rules require that all items of value received by participating members in connection with a public offering be included in the calculation of underwriting compensation. Structuring payments as 'advisory services agreements' to circumvent compensation caps and disclosure requirements is precisely the type of evasion the CF Rules are designed to prevent. Regulatory Notice 24-17 and proposed amendments to the CF Rules reaffirm that all forms of compensation connected to an offering must be captured, and the firm's failure to include these payments constitutes both a disclosure violation and a potential fraud on investors.

HYPOTHETICAL 790 | COMPLIANT | 15_FINRA_Regulatory_Notices
============================================================

FACTS
A 78-year-old retired teacher, Harold, with a $280,000 account requests an immediate $95,000 withdrawal to purchase a vacation property. His financial advisor, noting the large withdrawal relative to account size and Harold's age, contacts the trusted contact person listed on Harold's account—his adult daughter—to verify Harold's intent and confirm there are no concerns about undue third-party influence. The daughter confirms she is aware of the purchase and supports her father's decision. The advisor documents the conversation with the trusted contact person, notes Harold's clear capacity and independent decision-making during in-person meetings, and processes the withdrawal within three business days. The firm's compliance system logs the temporary hold review and trusted contact outreach.

QUESTION
Did the advisor and firm comply with FINRA rules when they contacted the trusted contact person and briefly delayed the disbursement before processing the senior client's large withdrawal request?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

FINRA Rule 4512 requires firms to make reasonable efforts to obtain trusted contact person information, and Rule 2165 authorizes firms to place temporary holds on disbursements when there is a reasonable belief of potential financial exploitation of a senior. Here, the advisor acted prudently by contacting the trusted contact person to verify the legitimacy of a large withdrawal by an elderly client, documented the outreach and the client's capacity, and processed the withdrawal promptly once concerns were resolved. This is exactly the type of protective yet client-respecting conduct FINRA's senior investor rules are designed to encourage.

HYPOTHETICAL 806 | NON-COMPLIANT | 11_Case_Law
============================================================

FACTS
Greatland Corporation established a 401(k) profit-sharing plan for its 2,200 employees with approximately $340 million in assets. The plan's Investment Committee, chaired by the company's CFO, selected Greatland Securities, Inc.—a wholly-owned broker-dealer subsidiary—as the exclusive provider of investment management services for all plan assets. The subsidiary charged a 0.85% annual asset-based fee for managing proprietary mutual funds within the plan, while comparable index funds from third-party providers were available at 0.04%–0.12%. The Investment Committee conducted no independent evaluation of alternative providers and did not document any analysis of whether the subsidiary's fees were reasonable relative to market alternatives. Over a seven-year period, the plan paid approximately $18.2 million in excess fees to the affiliated subsidiary.

QUESTION
Did the plan's Investment Committee violate ERISA's prohibited transaction rules and fiduciary duties by directing all plan assets to a corporate affiliate without conducting an independent fee analysis?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is not compliant. This constitutes self-dealing in violation of ERISA § 406(b) and a breach of the duty of prudence under ERISA § 404(a)(1)(B).

Under ERISA § 406(b)(1), a fiduciary may not deal with plan assets in his own interest or for his own account. In Acosta v. City National Corp., the Ninth Circuit affirmed liability where a corporate fiduciary channeled plan assets to an affiliated entity without an adequate independent process. Here, the Investment Committee directed $340 million exclusively to a corporate subsidiary charging fees far exceeding market rates, without any documented analysis of alternatives—mirroring the self-dealing found impermissible in City National. The duty of prudence further required a thorough, independent investigation of available options, which was entirely absent.

HYPOTHETICAL 807 | COMPLIANT | 11_Case_Law
============================================================

FACTS
Meridian Energy Corp. underwent a corporate spin-off in 2018, separating from its parent company, Atlas Petroleum Corp. As part of the separation, the Meridian Employee Savings Plan's Investment Committee was required to manage a significant holding of legacy Atlas Petroleum stock that remained in the plan. Over the next 30 months, the Committee engaged an independent investment consultant to evaluate the continued inclusion of Atlas stock. The consultant produced quarterly reports analyzing Atlas's financial health, stock volatility, and concentration risk. Based on these analyses, the Committee adopted a phased divestiture strategy, reducing Atlas stock from 28% of plan assets to under 4% over the 30-month period. Two plan participants filed suit alleging the Committee breached its ERISA fiduciary duty by failing to divest Atlas stock immediately upon the spin-off, claiming the stock declined 15% during the transition period.

QUESTION
Did the Investment Committee breach its ERISA fiduciary duty of prudence by implementing a phased divestiture of the legacy parent-company stock rather than divesting immediately?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant. The Investment Committee's deliberate, well-documented phased divestiture, supported by an independent consultant, satisfies the duty of prudence.

In Schweitzer v. Investment Committee of the Phillips 66 Savings Plan, the Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal of claims alleging fiduciary breach for failure to immediately divest legacy parent-company stock following a corporate spin-off, recognizing that fiduciaries are entitled to a reasonable process and timeframe for evaluating divestiture decisions. Here, unlike in Schweitzer where plaintiffs failed to state a claim, the Committee affirmatively engaged an independent consultant, generated quarterly analyses, and executed a systematic reduction from 28% to under 4%—demonstrating the type of deliberate, informed process that satisfies ERISA's prudent-expert standard. A short-term 15% stock decline during an orderly liquidation does not establish imprudence when the fiduciary's decision-making process was thorough and well-documented.

HYPOTHETICAL 808 | NON-COMPLIANT | 13_FINRA_Rulebook
============================================================

FACTS
A registered representative at a FINRA member firm recommends that Margaret Chen, a 74-year-old retired schoolteacher with $210,000 in liquid assets and a stated investment objective of capital preservation, exchange her existing deferred variable annuity — which has exited its surrender period — for a new deferred variable annuity with a 7-year surrender schedule and an annual mortality and expense charge 35 basis points higher than her current contract. Did the registered representative and supervising principal comply with FINRA Rule 2330 (formerly Rule 2821) requirements for the recommended variable annuity exchange?

ANSWER
No, this conduct violates FINRA Rule 2330's suitability and principal review requirements for deferred variable annuity exchanges.

FINRA Rule 2330(b) requires that, before recommending a deferred variable annuity exchange, the representative must have a reasonable basis to believe the customer has been informed of the material features of both the existing and proposed annuities — including surrender charges, fees, and benefits — and that the exchange is suitable considering the customer's age, liquidity needs, investment objectives, and the costs of the new surrender period. Rule 2330(c) further requires that a registered principal review and approve the transaction before submission based on documentation that demonstrates the exchange meets these suitability criteria. Here, the representative failed to perform or document a comparative analysis of the two contracts, and the principal rubber-stamped the exchange without the required substantive review, violating both provisions.

HYPOTHETICAL 809 | COMPLIANT | 13_FINRA_Rulebook
============================================================

FACTS
David Nowak, a 58-year-old small business owner with a $1.8 million investment portfolio, an annual income of $325,000, and a stated risk tolerance of moderate-to-aggressive, contacts his registered representative at a FINRA member firm and asks to allocate $150,000 (approximately 8% of his portfolio) into a leveraged ETF that tracks the S&P 500 at 2x daily returns. The representative, aware of the product's complexity, conducts and documents reasonable diligence into the leveraged ETF's mechanics — including its daily reset feature, volatility decay risk, and unsuitability for long-term buy-and-hold strategies. The representative explains these risks in detail to David, documents that David has 30 years of active trading experience including prior use of leveraged and inverse products, and confirms David's intent to use the position as a short-term tactical allocation with a 30-day target holding period. The representative documents the entire conversation, David's acknowledgment of the risks, and the rationale for why the allocation is consistent with David's overall portfolio profile, objectives, and experience. The firm's supervisory system flags the trade for heightened review, and the supervising principal reviews and approves the transaction after examining the representative's documentation.

QUESTION
Does the representative's recommendation of a leveraged ETF satisfy the reasonable-basis, customer-specific, and quantitative suitability obligations under FINRA Rule 2111?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

Under the reasonable-basis obligation of Rule 2111, the representative performed reasonable diligence to understand the leveraged ETF's nature, risks, and mechanics — including daily reset and volatility decay — satisfying the requirement that there be an investment rationale and that the product not be recommended without understanding. Under the customer-specific obligation, the recommendation was tailored to David's documented profile: substantial net worth, high income, moderate-to-aggressive risk tolerance, decades of experience with complex products, and a short-term tactical intent consistent with how leveraged ETFs are designed to perform. The 8% portfolio allocation is proportionate to the client's overall wealth and risk capacity. The firm's supervisory procedures under Rule 3110 also functioned properly, with the flagged trade receiving documented principal review.

FACTS

Additionally, FINRA Rule 3110 requires member firms to establish and maintain supervisory systems reasonably designed to achieve compliance — the branch manager's perfunctory initialing of concentration exception reports without follow-up action constitutes a supervisory failure consistent with patterns seen in FINRA arbitration awards such as Case 16-01819 involving customer claims against broker-dealers in St. Louis.

HYPOTHETICAL 814 | NON-COMPLIANT | 14_NASAA_State_Enforcement
============================================================

FACTS
Raymond James Financial Services, Inc. ('RJFS') executed approximately 270,000 low-principal equity transactions in customer accounts across multiple states, including Massachusetts, between 2018 and 2022. On these transactions, RJFS charged commissions that, when calculated as a percentage of the transaction's principal value, frequently exceeded 5% and in some cases reached 20–30% of principal on trades involving balances under $500. The Massachusetts Securities Division, acting as lead state in a coordinated investigation, found that the commission structure was applied systematically without individualized review of whether such charges were reasonable relative to the services rendered, the size of the transaction, or comparable market rates. RJFS's written supervisory procedures did not include any mechanism to flag, review, or reject commission charges that were disproportionate to transaction principal. The Division entered a Consent Order under Docket No. E-2023-0041 requiring remediation and a fine.

QUESTION
Did RJFS's practice of charging commissions that frequently exceeded 5%—and sometimes 20–30%—of principal on low-value equity transactions violate Massachusetts state securities law?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is not compliant — it constitutes charging unreasonable commissions in violation of the Massachusetts Uniform Securities Act.

The Massachusetts Uniform Securities Act and its implementing regulations prohibit broker-dealers from charging unreasonable commissions that are disproportionate to the services provided and the size of the transaction. On low-principal equity trades, a commission consuming 20–30% of transaction value is facially unreasonable under the NASAA Statement of Policy on Dishonest or Unethical Business Practices, which identifies excessive markups and commissions as a per se violation. RJFS's failure to implement supervisory controls capable of identifying and preventing these charges compounded the substantive violation, as coordinated state enforcement—led by Massachusetts—confirmed across approximately 270,000 transactions.

HYPOTHETICAL 815 | COMPLIANT | 14_NASAA_State_Enforcement
============================================================

FACTS
Meridian Capital Advisors, LLC is a state-registered investment adviser with $87 million in assets under management, currently registered with the California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation ('DFPI') and examined by state regulators as part of the 2025 NASAA Coordinated Investment Adviser Examination program conducted between February 1 and July 31, 2025. During the examination—the first such examination Meridian had undergone as a state-registered firm—examiners noted that two of Meridian's investment adviser representatives ('IARs') had recently passed the Series 65 examination and were provisionally listed on Form ADV Part 1 before their individual IAR applications were fully processed by the IARD system, a processing delay of 11 business days caused by a documented IARD system backlog. QUESTION

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

California and NASAA model rules require that IAR applications be filed through the IARD system prior to or contemporaneously with the commencement of advisory activities, but enforcement practice and DFPI guidance distinguish between a failure to file and a ministerial processing delay outside the firm's control. Meridian's compliance officer submitted applications and funded the IARD daily account contemporaneously with the IARs beginning work, satisfying the firm's affirmative regulatory obligation to initiate registration. Because the IARs did not solicit new clients and operated exclusively under the supervision of a fully registered principal during the processing window, no investor was exposed to the risks that registration requirements are designed to prevent. A registered broker-dealer, Meridian Capital Advisors, recommends that a 72-year-old retired schoolteacher with $180,000 in savings and a stated conservative risk tolerance roll her entire IRA into a variable annuity with a 7-year surrender period and annual fees of 2.85%. The broker, Marcus Tilden, earns a $9,000 commission on the transaction. When the client asks whether Marcus has any financial interest in the recommendation, he tells her the product is 'no extra cost to her' and never discloses the commission or surrender charges. The Dodd-Frank Act §913 study explicitly flagged broker compensation conflicts as a primary investor harm requiring enhanced disclosure obligations under any uniform fiduciary or best interest standard.

QUESTION
Did Marcus Tilden's failure to disclose his $9,000 commission and the 7-year surrender period to his retired client violate applicable conduct standards?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is a material conflict-of-interest disclosure violation under Reg BI and the Dodd-Frank §913 investor protection framework.

The Dodd-Frank §913 study identified broker compensation conflicts as a central investor harm and directed the SEC to establish rules ensuring brokers act in clients' best interest with full conflict disclosure. Reg BI's Conflict of Interest Obligation requires broker-dealers to establish policies to identify, disclose, and mitigate conflicts including compensation-based incentives. Affirmatively misrepresenting that a product has 'no extra cost' while concealing a $9,000 commission compounds the disclosure violation into potential fraud under Exchange Act antifraud provisions.

HYPOTHETICAL 830 | COMPLIANT | 16_Congressional_Materials

FACTS

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

Trentwood satisfied the disclosure prong through plain-English ADV disclosure with dollar-range estimates and augmented it with transaction-level statement disclosures. The firm satisfied the best-interest prong by establishing a quarterly best-execution committee that documented the affiliated-clearing cost is within 0.4 basis points of unaffiliated alternatives, meeting the standard that best execution does not require the lowest possible cost but the most favorable terms reasonably obtainable. GAO reports have specifically cited this type of proactive audit-and-remediate compliance model as consistent with robust fiduciary practice.

The representative completes a Best Interest Analysis documenting the client's 20-year investment horizon, high risk tolerance, $800,000 in other diversified assets held at other institutions, her professional sophistication, and the speculative nature and volatility profile of the specific biotech issuer. The representative also documents a verbal warning given to the client regarding concentration risk and the potential for total loss, confirms the investment represents 25% of the accounts he can observe, and notes the client's unsolicited initiation of the request. He then executes the transaction and retains the completed analysis in the client file.

QUESTION
Does the representative's handling of the client's request to concentrate $300,000 in a single biotech issuer satisfy Reg BI's Care Obligation?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

Reg BI's Care Obligation applies to recommendations, and while the client initiated the request, the representative still made a recommendation by agreeing to execute. However, the Care Obligation is satisfied when the representative conducts a thorough, documented analysis of the specific client's full financial profile, including assets held away, risk tolerance, and time horizon. The documentation of the client's professional sophistication, other diversified holdings, long investment horizon, and the explicit risk warning satisfies the requirement to have a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation is in this specific client's best interest. The SEC's guidance acknowledges that concentration in higher-risk securities may be appropriate for certain high-net-worth, sophisticated clients when properly documented.

HYPOTHETICAL 845 | COMPLIANT | 17_SEC_Staff_Bulletins

FACTS

Form CRS is delivered at account opening, disclosing that the advisory account generates ongoing fees to the firm regardless of trading activity and that this creates an incentive to recommend the advisory account over a brokerage account. The representative's written account-type analysis documents that, at the anticipated trading frequency, the commission-based alternative would generate approximately $1,800 annually versus $6,750 under the advisory structure, and concludes that the advisory account's comprehensive financial planning services, tax-loss harvesting, and automatic rebalancing justify the higher cost for this client's retirement accumulation goals. The analysis is reviewed and approved by the branch compliance officer.

QUESTION
Does the representative's recommendation of the higher-cost advisory account over a less expensive brokerage account satisfy Reg BI's Care and Conflict of Interest Obligations despite the firm's financial incentive to recommend advisory accounts?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

Reg BI expressly applies to recommendations of account types, requiring that the recommendation be in the retail customer's best interest after considering the customer's investment profile and the costs, risks, and benefits of each account type. The SEC's guidance acknowledges that a higher-cost account type may be in the client's best interest when qualitative benefits such as planning services and rebalancing provide genuine value relative to the client's specific goals. The firm satisfies the Conflict of Interest Obligation by specifically disclosing the financial incentive in Form CRS and by requiring documented cost-benefit analysis reviewed by a compliance officer, constituting a structural mitigation measure rather than mere acknowledgment of the conflict. The written analysis quantifying the $4,950 annual cost differential and articulating service-based justifications provides a defensible, client-specific basis for the recommendation.

HYPOTHETICAL 847 | NON-COMPLIANT | 17_SEC_Staff_Bulletins
============================================================

FACTS

Okafor's firm has a revenue-sharing arrangement with Clearstream Mutual Funds whereby Clearstream pays Prestige 12b-1 fees averaging 0.75% annually on assets placed in Clearstream's Class A shares. Internal firm policy acknowledges this conflict in a generic disclosure buried in Prestige's Form ADV Part 2A but does not require representatives to affirmatively discuss the conflict with clients at the point of recommendation, nor does the firm have any mitigation mechanism such as a preference for lower-cost share classes. Okafor recommends Clearstream Class A shares to 14 clients in 2022, including seven for whom no-load institutional share classes of equivalent funds were available at materially lower cost within the same platform.

QUESTION
Does Prestige Wealth Advisors' conflict management framework satisfy its obligations under Reg BI and the SEC's fiduciary duty framework for investment advisers regarding the 12b-1 fee revenue-sharing arrangement?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is a violation of Reg BI's Conflict of Interest Obligation and the investment adviser duty of loyalty under the Advisers Act fiduciary standard.

The SEC's 2023 Conflicts Staff Bulletin and the Fiduciary Interpretation make clear that generic, buried disclosure of financial conflicts does not satisfy the duty of loyalty; advisers must identify, manage, and mitigate material conflicts, not merely disclose them. Under Reg BI's Conflict of Interest Obligation, broker-dealers must establish policies to identify and mitigate conflicts that provide an incentive to place client interests secondary to their own, which includes revenue-sharing arrangements like 12b-1 fees. Where lower-cost equivalent share classes are available on the same platform, recommending the higher-cost class that generates firm revenue without any mitigation mechanism—such as a share-class selection policy—constitutes a failure to act in the retail customer's best interest. The IAA Conflicts CLE materials confirm that identifying, managing, and disclosing conflicts are distinct and cumulative obligations, not alternatives.

HYPOTHETICAL 848 | NON-COMPLIANT | 17_SEC_Staff_Bulletins

The Care Obligation under Reg BI requires a representative to have a reasonable basis to believe a recommendation is in the best interest of the particular retail customer based on their investment profile, including financial situation, risk tolerance, and investment objectives. The 2022 SEC Staff Bulletin emphasizes that representatives must understand the risks of complex products and assess whether those risks are consistent with the customer's profile before recommending them. A 3x leveraged ETF's daily reset compounding and volatility decay make it unsuitable as a long-term investment for a moderate risk-tolerance investor, and concentrating 60% of liquid net worth in a single leveraged instrument compounds the failure. HYPOTHETICAL 861 | NON-COMPLIANT | 18_OCC_Bank_Trust_Guidance
============================================================

FACTS
Heartland Savings Association's trust department manages a $4.7 million ERISA-qualified defined benefit pension plan for a regional manufacturing company with 200 participants. The trust department's investment committee recommends directing $800,000 of plan assets into a proprietary money market fund managed by Heartland's affiliated asset management subsidiary, which charges a 0.45% annual management fee — higher than comparable unaffiliated funds charging 0.08–0.12%. The bank discloses the affiliated relationship in the plan's annual fee disclosure but does not document any independent fiduciary analysis demonstrating that the affiliated fund's terms are at least as favorable as those available from unaffiliated providers. QUESTION
Does Heartland's allocation of ERISA plan assets to its affiliated proprietary fund without documented independent fiduciary analysis satisfy its conflict-of-interest obligations under OCC and ERISA standards?

The OCC Conflicts of Interest handbook specifically addresses 'Dealings With Affiliated Service Providers and Allocation of Brokerage Services to Affiliates,' requiring that transactions with affiliates be on terms at least as favorable as those available from unaffiliated parties and be supported by documented independent analysis. Heartland's affiliated fund charged a fee four to five times higher than comparable unaffiliated alternatives, and no independent fiduciary analysis was prepared or retained. Under ERISA Section 406(b), a fiduciary is prohibited from dealing with plan assets in its own interest or acting in a transaction involving the plan on behalf of a party whose interests are adverse to plan participants, and a mere annual disclosure without substantive analysis does not constitute an adequate exemption.

Does Atlas National Bank's allocation of 14.3% of a charitable remainder unitrust to an unaffiliated private credit fund, pursuant to board-approved policy and documented committee review, comply with OCC fiduciary investment standards despite the illiquid nature of the asset?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

The OCC Asset Management handbook and operations and controls guidance recognize that alternative and illiquid investments are permissible in fiduciary accounts when the bank has established board-approved policies authorizing such allocations, the investment policy statement for the specific account permits the asset class, and the trust committee documents a thorough analysis of liquidity risk relative to the trust's distribution obligations. Atlas's 36-month liquidity stress analysis directly addressed the key risk for a CRUT with mandatory annual payouts, the 14.3% allocation was within the board-approved 20% ceiling, and the absence of any affiliated party compensation eliminates conflict-of-interest concerns. The documented committee deliberation and approval reflect the sound governance process OCC examiners assess under management and operations standards, and the use of an unaffiliated manager further insulates the decision from self-dealing scrutiny.

A registered CPO operates a commodity pool that holds interests in a global asset management holding company structure, which in turn owns operating subsidiaries across real estate and infrastructure sectors. The CPO's compliance team receives an inquiry questioning whether the intermediate holding companies within the structure—which do not themselves solicit commodity pool participants or pool funds for trading—must independently register as CPOs. The CPO obtains an interpretive letter from the CFTC Division of Swap Dealer and Intermediary Oversight, consistent with the analytical framework of CFTC Letter No. 17-68, confirming that intermediate holding companies that do not independently satisfy the definition of 'commodity pool' under CEA Section 1a(10) and CFTC Regulation 4.10(d)(1) need not register as CPOs.

QUESTION
Was the CPO's reliance on an interpretive no-action letter from the CFTC Division of Swap Dealer and Intermediary Oversight to determine that intermediate holding companies in its fund structure need not independently register as CPOs consistent with applicable CFTC requirements?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

CFTC Letter No. 17-68 establishes the Division's interpretive framework that entities within a multi-tier holding structure do not independently constitute commodity pools merely by virtue of owning interests in an entity that does qualify as a pool, where those holding entities do not themselves pool participant funds for commodity trading purposes. Reliance on a formal interpretive letter from the Division of Swap Dealer and Intermediary Oversight provides a recognized safe harbor from enforcement action under CFTC policy. The CPO's proactive approach of seeking and obtaining written interpretive guidance—rather than unilaterally assuming the exemption applied—represents a best practice in regulatory compliance.

HYPOTHETICAL 899 | COMPLIANT | 19_CFTC_Guidance
============================================================

FACTS
A registered CTA manages a futures trading program under CFTC Rule 4.7 for a pool consisting exclusively of QEPs, all of whom have securities and futures portfolios exceeding the current Portfolio Requirement financial thresholds. The program employs a contrarian strategy—entering long positions when contract prices decline and short positions when prices rise—consistent with documented retail futures trading behavioral patterns. A sophisticated institutional QEP participant with $12 million in qualifying assets challenges the suitability of the strategy after sustaining $215,000 in losses across seven trades, arguing the CTA failed to adequately explain downside risk. The CTA produces documentation showing that its pre-investment disclosure package included a detailed description of the contrarian strategy, historical drawdown scenarios, margin requirements, and signed acknowledgment from the participant, and that it filed all required CPO-PQR reports with the CFTC for the relevant reporting periods.

QUESTION
Did the CTA satisfy its disclosure and suitability obligations to the QEP institutional participant despite the participant's subsequent trading losses?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

For pools operated exclusively for QEPs under Rule 4.7, CTAs and CPOs benefit from reduced but not eliminated disclosure obligations, and the CTA here exceeded those requirements by providing detailed strategy-specific risk disclosures and obtaining written acknowledgment. CFTC research confirms that contrarian futures strategies—entering long on price declines and short on price increases—represent a recognized and documented trading approach, not an inherently unsuitable one for sophisticated participants. The institutional participant's $12 million QEP-qualifying portfolio, combined with the documented pre-investment disclosure and the CTA's current CPO-PQR reporting, demonstrates that the regulatory framework was followed even though losses materialized. Post-hoc trading losses do not retroactively establish a suitability violation where adequate disclosure and participant sophistication were present at inception.

HYPOTHETICAL 900 | NON-COMPLIANT | 20_SEC_ALJ_OALJ_Decisions
============================================================

FACTS
Drew Horton, the sole principal of Horton Investment Management LLC, a registered investment adviser managing approximately $180 million in client assets, directed his supervised representatives to recommend proprietary wrap-fee programs to clients without disclosing that the firm received additional compensation from the program sponsors. Between 2018 and 2021, at least 47 retail clients, including several retirees living on fixed incomes, were placed into these wrap programs at annual fees of 2.25%, generating approximately $890,000 in undisclosed compensation to the firm. Horton received written internal complaints from two representatives questioning the disclosures but took no remedial action. The firm's Form ADV Part 2A failed to disclose the material conflict of interest arising from these revenue-sharing arrangements.

QUESTION
Does Horton Investment Management's failure to disclose revenue-sharing compensation from wrap-fee program sponsors in its Form ADV, combined with Horton's failure to act on internal supervisory red flags, constitute a violation of the Investment Advisers Act?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is a violation of Investment Advisers Act §206(2) and §207, and constitutes a supervisory failure under §203(e) and §203(f).

Section 206(2) prohibits an investment adviser from engaging in any transaction, practice, or course of business that operates as a fraud or deceit upon a client, including material omissions of conflicts of interest. Failure to disclose revenue-sharing arrangements in Form ADV Part 2A constitutes a materially false filing under §207. The ALJ in Horter imposed civil penalties and a supervisory collateral bar precisely because the principal ignored internal warning signs, demonstrating willful disregard of supervisory obligations under §203(e) and §203(f).

HYPOTHETICAL 901 | NON-COMPLIANT | 20_SEC_ALJ_OALJ_Decisions
============================================================

FACTS
Nicholas Sarto, a registered representative at a mid-size broker-dealer, was convicted in federal district court of wire fraud in connection with a scheme to divert $215,000 from elderly client accounts by forging withdrawal forms and directing proceeds to a personal bank account. Following his conviction, Sarto's broker-dealer did not file a Uniform Termination Notice and Sarto continued to appear on the firm's books as a registered representative for 90 days post-conviction. During this period, Sarto solicited two new clients, a 74-year-old retired nurse and a 68-year-old veteran, and collected $18,500 in new account fees. The firm's compliance department had received the court's sentencing document but failed to route it to the registration department.

QUESTION
Does a broker-dealer's failure to terminate a registered representative's association following a federal fraud conviction, thereby allowing continued client solicitation, constitute a violation of Exchange Act Section 15(b)?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is a statutory disqualification violation under Exchange Act §15(b)(4) and §15(b)(6), and constitutes a supervision failure exposing the firm to sanctions.

Exchange Act §15(b)(4)(B) mandates that a broker-dealer may not maintain association with a person subject to statutory disqualification, which includes criminal convictions for securities fraud or fraud involving financial transactions. As illustrated in Skaltsounis, the Commission will impose a permanent bar on individuals convicted of fraud, and broker-dealers that knowingly or negligently maintain such associations face independent sanctions. The firm's failure to route the sentencing document through compliance reflects a systemic supervisory breakdown that allowed a disqualified person to continue harming retail investors.

HYPOTHETICAL 902 | NON-COMPLIANT | 20_SEC_ALJ_OALJ_Decisions
============================================================

FACTS
Suzanne Bellamy, a portfolio manager at a registered investment adviser overseeing a $45 million equity mutual fund, executed a series of cross-trades between the fund and a separate private client account she personally managed, routing $3.2 million in underperforming small-cap positions from the private account into the fund at prices slightly above market close without seeking independent valuation or board approval. Bellamy disclosed the cross-trades to her supervisor in a brief email but did not disclose her personal financial interest — she owned a 12% carried interest in the private account — in the fund's Form N-CEN or the clients' account statements. The fund's independent directors were never informed of the transactions. An internal audit 14 months later revealed that the cross-traded securities declined an average of 31% within six months of transfer, resulting in approximately $992,000 in fund losses.

QUESTION
Does a portfolio manager's execution of undisclosed cross-trades between a mutual fund and a private account in which she holds a personal financial interest, without board approval or independent valuation, violate the Investment Advisers Act and Investment Company Act?

ANSWER
No, this conduct is a fraudulent scheme under Investment Advisers Act §206(1) and §206(2), and violates Investment Company Act §17(a) prohibiting affiliated transactions without exemptive relief.

Section 206(1) prohibits intentional fraud on clients, and §206(2) prohibits any practice operating as a deceit, both of which are implicated when a manager self-deals by transferring deteriorating assets from a personally beneficial account into a client fund. Investment Company Act §17(a) flatly prohibits affiliated persons from selling securities to a registered fund unless an exemption under Rule 17a-7 is satisfied, which requires, inter alia, that transactions be at independent market price with no brokerage commission and that the board adopt procedures — conditions Bellamy did not meet. The failure to disclose her carried interest to the fund's directors compounded the fraud, as established in proceedings mirroring the Ballek matter under §203(f) and §9(b) of the Investment Company Act.

HYPOTHETICAL 903 | COMPLIANT | 20_SEC_ALJ_OALJ_Decisions
============================================================

FACTS
A registered investment adviser, Meridian Capital Advisors LLC, manages separate accounts for 23 institutional clients and 8 high-net-worth individuals. In 2023, Meridian began recommending a thinly traded micro-cap issuer, Pacifica Protein Corp., to clients after conducting 60 hours of proprietary research, including management interviews, supply chain analysis, and review of three years of audited financials. Meridian's Form ADV Part 2A disclosed that the firm's research analysts personally held positions in securities the firm recommended, and that Meridian had a policy requiring a 72-hour pre-clearance blackout period before and after client transactions. Two analysts owned Pacifica shares worth $14,200 and $9,800 respectively, disclosed under the policy, and all client purchases were executed after the blackout period. The firm's CCO documented the research basis and conflict mitigation steps in contemporaneous written records.

QUESTION
Does Meridian Capital Advisors' recommendation of a micro-cap security in which its analysts hold personal positions constitute a disqualifying conflict of interest under the Investment Advisers Act, notwithstanding the firm's disclosure and pre-clearance procedures?

ANSWER
Yes, this conduct is compliant.

Rule 204A-1 requires registered investment advisers to adopt a code of ethics that includes personal trading pre-clearance procedures and reporting requirements, but does not prohibit analysts from holding positions in recommended securities provided conflicts are properly disclosed and managed. Meridian's 72-hour blackout period, advance disclosure in Form ADV, and contemporaneous documentation of the research basis and conflict mitigation satisfy the rule's requirements. The relatively modest personal holdings ($14,200 and $9,800) further weigh against a finding of material undisclosed conflict, as the analysts lacked sufficient position size to materially benefit from client-driven price movement in a manner that would operate as a deceit under §206(2).
